The result of free trade, as a doctrine to be invoked in opposition to this resolution, is that in the greatest manufacturing country in the world; in the richest country in the world; in a country where the manufacturers are overflowing with wealth, the labouring classes of the highest rank earn only thirty-three shillings and eleven pence per week on an average. Under these cir-iumstances, is it surprising that Mr. Snowden, representing the labouring classes, moved in the Imperial House of Coni mons on the the 3rd of March last, an amendment to the Speech from the Throne:
Expressing regret that in view of the existing industrial and social conditions of lal-ge masses of the people arising from a de

so fond of referring as the typical exponent of the advantages of free trade, the people are paying from $350,000,000 or $360,000,000 a year in taxes or duties on what they eat, drink and smoke, it hardly seems fair to talk about free trade in England. I venture to say that there is no place on the face of the earth, except in darkest Africa or in the remotest sections of Asia, in which true and genuine free trade in its full application is known or practiced.

It has been my firm conviction for years that one of the main desires and purposes of the protected interests has been to becloud the thought and befuddle the thinker, and I think my hon. friend (Mr. Northrup), in the dissertation he has given us, has lived up to that principle. I spent two hours thinking what he said and meant, and then I had Only a rough guess as to what he was really driving at. Now that he has talked for twenty minutes more, I am hopelessly in the dark to know what his argument is. Possibly' the Minister of Finance, having sojourned with two schools of thought, Liberal and Conservative, may be able to take the true sense of the arguments of the hon. member for East Hastings and classify and divide them in some way so as to make head or tail of them. About the only clear thing I understood him to state was that there was no such thing as protection.

The hon. member
certainly did not.
That no such thing was in order in this House.

I thought he said he
was in favour of a reduction of the tariff.
I understood him to say that any talk about high protection in this House was out of order as much as it would be to talk in Gaelic or in German.

I certainly did say
that.

Even then I did not know why he said that. Tariff has been talked in this House probably before any of us were members of the House and why the hon. member should state it was out of order to talk about protection because only English and French can be spoken in this House-
The hon. member is unintentionally misrepresenting me. I did not say it was out of order to talk about this question, but I said that to speak of high protection is not good English.

I will have to withdraw that then and to say that I have not the faintest idea of what he intends to convey. He did not even go so far as to tell Mr. NORTHRUP.
us what adequate protection was. I presume he will classify that as being something that is out of order.
That would he protection, that is good English.

I think protection is
out of order anywhere and should not be tolerated. My hon. friend prefaced his remarks by misrepresenting me inadvertently. I think he made that the occasion for rising to speak. He stated that by asking a question of the Finance Minister as to how it was any monetary advantage to the province of Saskatchewan that there should be an industry like this in British Columbia, I was giving another manifestation of my lack of patriotism and of loyalty. Let me remind you that I distinctly said: What monetary advantage in addition to the gratification which comes to all of us through our natural pride in seeing our brother Canadians prosperous in British Columbia. After my having it put on those broad lines it was not the most magnanimous or graceful thing for the hon. member to speak of lack of loyalty because I had asked a question.
The minister said it would be an advantage to Saskatchewan; and, knowing the great tendency of hon. gentlemen opposite to impugn our loyalty and patriotism, I was careful to say that I recognized the advantage due our fellow-Canadians as a great benefit; but even after that he could not miss the chance to gather the flag about him and give us a biff in the eye about lack of patriotism. I have always found from what little reading or observation I have been able to employ that the only way you are ever going to get a patriotic and loyal people in Canada is, as in any other country, by using all the people fairly and making them a contented people. Then you will have a loyal people and I think that a policy such as he advocates, that takes away from one class, the ordinary, common people, their right to trade where they like in the open markets of the world, is not calculated to bring about the existence of a contented or loyal people on the prairie* of the Dominion of Canada. My hon friend has given us some remarkbable instances from the economic history of Great Britain. If I came anywhere within following dis tance of him-and I admit that I lost him in the haze many times-his reasoning comes to this, that the manufacturer in Great Britain established himself and developed his industry so successfully under protection in the early part of the nineteenth century that he was getting on too well and he put on the brake of free trade for fear he would get too rich.
I certainly said nothing of the! kind.
They never had free trade; they have not got it yet.

The hon. member will
have to enlighten us; he will have to make a new dictionary, glossary and everything. If they have not free trade in Great Britain, I am entirely at sea. I understand they have free trade in Great Britain. The ground taken by my hon. friend was that free trade was rotten in Great Britain and he proved inductively that that was so. Now he doubles on his tracks and says they have mot got free trade in Great Britain. If they have not got free trade there, then I curse the protection which brought about those conditions in Great Britain.
I am glad you admit them, at all events.

I am giving my time and attention to developing the good things in this country and I am not spending my time in digging up information unfavourable to Great Britain and spreading it on * Hansard.' If my understanding of it is correct, my hon. friend's argument, when sifted, comes to this and it turns entirely against himself, that Great Britain has prospered in an unexampled degree under free trade, whereas, under protection, she was practically stagnant. He talked about the wages given there. As my hon. friend from Red Deer pointed out, President Woodrow Wilson, time and again in the late elections, made the statement, which was never contradicted, that the wool workers in Lawrence, Massachusetts, were working for one dollar a day, certainly for wages lower than they had in Great Britain.
That is why they struck.

Did my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) tell ns what wages they got in Great Britain under protection ? If he compared the wages paid under protection in Great Britain with those paid under free trade, he would find that the former were starvation wages. Perhaps the working classes in Great Britain do not get enough to-day. The social conditions in Great Britain are not ideal. They arise from the most unfortunate and unjust class system of centralizing all the wealth. Protection is going to bring the same class system in our

country, the centralization of immense fortunes. The poverty in Great Britain, to which my hon. friend referred, is due to the class system of centralizing wealth and the holding of land in the hands of a few, and is not due to conditions of the tariff. The argument of my hon. friend goes to show that in so far as we may take any lesson from the history of Great Britain, it is that the sooner we develop along lines leading to the goal of free trade, towards the conditions which have made Great Britain prosperous and great in the world, the better it will be for us, and the longer we hold back, the more firmly will be established the bullying hold of the interests which lie so close to the Government that to-day occupies the treasury benches. My hon. friend from Bast Hastings said that it the people of Saskatchewan take the view that they should not abide by a tariff, we might as well give up Confederation. We do not take that stand at all. Let me state my position once and for all on the tariff. Within certain limits, we are ready to encourage the establishment of industries in Canada,-perhaps we cannot do anything else, because we are a small proportion-but it must be distinctly understood that we are prepared to do so voluntarily, and that no man in Toronto or in the Kootenays, has a right to make us pay for his maintenance. When our friends say that they have a right to put their hands in our pockets and take our money we protest. If we are asked to reason together, and to consent to a certain amount of protection, we are ready to reason with those men, but they have no right to come and say: I am making so much money out of my business, but it - is not enough, and we want to get a bounty, and we will put our hands in your pockets and make you give it to us. When the lead producers come to us and say you must give us two or three million dollars, to help us, you must pay us a better price for lumber, and you must be not only a market for us but a mark, we protest. The other day the hon. member from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) asked me whether it was not the case that the farmers on the prairies were prosperous, as if the fact that they were prosperous, was any reason why the lumbermen in British Columbia, or the men who make implements in Toronto or in any other part of Canada, have a right to take away our prosperity. It is the assumption on the part of those men that they have a right to take our money from us that makes our blood boil. We are gratified to see our fellow Canadians prosperous. To us it is a source of pride that we are building up a nation in Canada, but when our manufacturing friends come to the lobbies of this House, and endeavour to hold up Parliament, say-Mr. KNOWLES.
ing, we have had our graft and rake-offs and now we want you to help us more by putting your hands in your pockets, and if you do not, we will use the bludgeon, then we rebel.
I should like to ask my hon. friend why he did not make this speech in 1908?

I made stronger
speeches than this along that line.
They are not in 'Hansard.' I do not remember seeing any speech of yours against this bounty.
I do not know whether I was in the House or not. But I am not opposing the bounty very strongly.
Oh, oh.

There need not be any oh's about it. The protected interests deal in befuddling arguments, Dut I have said in this House, and I could refer to my hon. friend to my very words, that I think protection an abomination, that I think it is a matter of trusts and combines and that it is a cause of loss in every country. I have said before in Parliament, and I say still, that I can best serve my constituency by supporting the party that makes for the lowering of the tariff. As between the two parties, I have no hesitation in giving my undivided support to the party that makes for the lowering of the tariff, and if my hon. friend will read what I have said in the past about the tariff, he will find that it was a good deal stronger than what I am saying to-day.
I have noticed that you always voted right.

The argument that has been made in favour of the resolution is based upon the assertion that the resolution is merely a continuation of the policy of the previous Government. It is true that the resolution proposes to dispose of a certain balance of an appropriation made by the previous Government for a specific purpose, but I want to point out that the conditions which existed when the late Government made the appropriation and provided for a bounty on lead, do not exist to-day, and, therefore, the reasons which existed then for the provision do not exist to-day. The argument that the present resolution is a continuation of the former policy is not well founded. I am aware that the strongest attack that our friends on the Government benches can make against the Opposition is that their policy is the same, and it is that form of attack to which I most strongly object. The bounty on lead was given at the time and under conditions as described by my hon. friend from Kootenay. The bounty

was justified by those conditions;-I will not put it that way, I will say that the bounty may have been justified by those conditions; it is immaterial whether the position is taken that it was or that it may have been justified. The conditions which the bounty was provided to meet having passed away, I maintain that the mere fact that the appropriation was not exhausted is no reason why my hon. friends on the Government benches should propose the continuance of the bounty.
Why does the hon. gentleman say that the conditions have changed and that the reason for granting the bounty has now passed away?

I am taking what my
hon. friend himself told the House, that when the bounty was granted the lead mining industry had practically ceased because of the low prices. The bounty was given and the lead mining industry was kept on its feet until an era of higher prices followed. The fact that the prices have been higher is proven absolutely and unquestionably by the further fact that the bounty was not exhausted, for if the prices had remained as they were when the bounty was voted, that bounty would have been exhausted long ago. The bounty was intended to carry the lead industry over a difficult situation, existing at that period. My hon. friend told the House in so many words-and he is thoroughly familiar with the facts and very frankly stated them to the House-that the bounty was granted for the purpose of carrying the lead mining industry over a difficult period. Having achieved its purpose and the period of difficulty having terminated, my hon. friend must take the responsibility of, as he says, continuing the bounty, but as a matter of fact of re-establishing the bounty and establishing it under the conditions of to-day which do not call for it. Only the amount of $600,000 is involved, and it is an amount, which, so to speak, has already been set aside for this purpose. But the argument that my hon. friend has made, and that has been taken up by all those who have spoken on the other side of the House, and has been to some extent, I may say, admitted on this side, is that he is merely continuing the policy of the late Liberal Government. It is that argument I want to protest against most emphatically; he is not continuing the policy of the late Liberal Government, he is taking upon himself to hand out, if the occasion shall arise-it may be that the occasion will not arise-the sum of $600,000 to the lead industry of Kootenay should the prices of lead go down. Remember, it was not merely because the prices of lead were down that the bounty was voted in the first place, it was to keep the lead industry from going out. it
was to keep it from sinking through the floor, under especially difficult circumstances. It was not a mere matter of taking so much money from the treasury of the Dominion of Canada and handing it over to the men who are mining the lead, which is my hon. friend's proposition of to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Although it
may not be spent.

That is exactly the point I want to argue, to a finish here and new, if I may be permitted. I am taking what my hon. friend from Kootenay says. I was a member of the House when the late bounty was given and am very familiar with the arguments in its behalf. I met the gentlemen from British Columbia who came here and argued in its favour. So, I am not speaking at random when I say that the bounty was given specifically to tide the lead industry over a diflieult period. It was not given for the purpose of bonusing lead mining in the Dominion of Canada as a permanent policy. Never was such an idea entertained, never was such a demand made on behalf of the lead mining industry, and if it had been made I am satisfied it would never have been conceded. I repeat, the request was made for the purpose of carrying the lead industry over a difficult period of its existence, and was not made for the purpose of establishing a policy of bonusing lead mining in Canada.
Does the hon. gentleman subscribe to the theory that these industries should be helped over just such trying periods?

I am inclined to think
that there are occasions when help may te given to an enterprise or industry in Canada with profit to the community. But I am not arguing against that; it 'eems to me that it is a fair proposition. Difficult circumstances may arise, and a particular industry may be of such importance

that it will warrant special assistance being given for a period to help it over a difficult time; but if it is said that this, that or the other industry is to get assistance out of the public treasury permanently in order to keep it alive, then I say, with my hon. friend from Moosejaw, that that industry has no claim upon the people of Canada to be kept alive, and it is cheaper for Canada, and better, for Canada, that it should go out of existence.
I have been trying to establish the point that is at issue between the two sides of the House, the difference between the policy of the late Government and the policy of the present Government in regard to this trifle of $600,000 to the lead industry. The question of bounties will come up; the question of protection will come up. I want to go on record here, at this particular time, and under these particular circumstances, as holding a certain, definite position. When the Government come forward with further proposals for the continuation of protection, either by bounty or duty, they will not be able to argue that, because we did it, they are entitled to it. What was done in the case of the lead bounty was done under special circumstances, these special circumstances have passed and the reason does not exist today. The Government are taking the responsibility of pursuing a policy of simply handing out of the public treasury money for the purpose of maintaining the profits of an established industry. If the lead industry of British Columbia, after having existed for a matter of fifteen years, is not now able to stand on its own feet, then it is not in a class that is entitled to special assistance and had better drop. My opinion is that the lead industry has arrived at a position when it can stand on its own feet, on its own merits, just the same as the production of wheat on the prairies has to stand on its own feet, and if it cannot, let the people who are mining lead take exactly the same advice as is given so freely to the people who are raising wheat who are told, if wheat raising is not profitable, to go into mixed farming. I suggest to the lead miner that he mine gold instead of lead.

The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) says very frankly that the bounty was given to the lead industry at a particular time when it was necessary, at least from the point of view of hon. gentlemen opposite, himself included, under certain conditions that then existed. He had said nothing to show that the conditions are materially different now. I claim that while the lead industry has undoubtedly benefited during the payment of this bounty, at the same time, it has not yet reached a position, in which it is able to stand upon its own merits.
As to the question of the low price of Mr. OLIVER.
lead, the hon. member for Edmonton must know that the lead market has not been at all steady, that it has had its ups and downs and it is simply to balance and steady the market that the bounty is given. If the hon. gentleman could assure this committee and the lead producers that the present price of lead will be maintained for the next five years, possibly there would be no need for this bounty being renewed, but we may be in the position, a month, or two months, or six months from now, of seeing the price of lead go down to where it was before and where it will be necessary, if the lead industry is going to exist at all, to pay this bounty.
There can be no question that the conditions of the lead market and of lead mining are such that the continuance of this bounty is essential. It is true that ten years ago the production of lead had almost ceased in British Columbia. To-day the production has reached a fair amount. But the men who have been in the lead producing business are only now commencing to get upon their feet, are only beginning to be in the position that we as Canadians want to have them in of being able to produce lead and to dispose of it in the world's markets. It must not be forgotten that the duties on lead and lead products coming into Canada are very low. I think that the duty on pig lead is fifteen per cent which, under the preferential tariff, is reduced to about ten per cent. That will hardly keep our own market for our own lead producers as against the mines of Spain, Mexico and countries where, labour and supplies being much cheaper, lead can be produced at a much lower rate. With the lead import duties so low and the cost of labour and provisions so high in Canada, the Government are pursuing the proper policy in extending this lead bounty. It matters not whether it was introduced by the former Government or this Government; I am not at all bothered about that, nor do I think that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is worried, whether he shall take the responsibility of it or not. I am quite sure that he is ready to do so because the conditions are such that it is necessary to have the bounty extended for a further term.

Mr. Chairman, I well remember the occasion when the law granting a bounty upon lead was enacted by this Parliament. Prior to 1903 many petitions were circulated throughout the province of Alberta. I remember signing one of those petitions, because I believed it was necessary for the reasons which have been given by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). If I am not mistaken all the agricultural organizations in southern Alberta signed that memorial which was presented to the Government

then in power. That memorial recited that if the lead industry were placed upon a sound and permanent basis it would secure for the farmers of southern Alberta a market for their products. After the bounty was given and after the industry was placed upon a sound basis there were three refrigerator cars per week carrying the products from the dairies and farms of Alberta into the Kootenay, while to-day that number has increased to one per day. I might inform my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that the town of Olds increased the quantity of butter and farm products that it shipped into the Kootenay very greatly by reason of the market which was created by .the construction of the smelter that was mentioned by my hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Green) which gives employment to a large number of men.
That was the principle upon which that bounty, amounting to a sum of $2,500,000, was granted. I am bound to say that by reason of the increase in the number of workmen employed in the British Columbia camps and smelting industries, we have a much greater demand for the agricultural products of the Lethbridge and southern Alberta districts and extending as far north as Lacombe. As a matter of fact, the demand goes as far north as Lacombe, it has spread to Stettler on the one branch and it has again spread to different points along the Alberta Irrigation and Railway Company's line. These products are,now being largely consumed at the points where smelters have been constructed and are being operated by reason of this bounty. There is an illustration of the benefits of protection given to a particular industry extending beyond the people to whom it was directly given. There is a case where protection has given a stimulus to the agricultural interests of southern Alberta. T recall the fact that the farmers of southern Alberta could not find a ready market for their products in British Columbia until such time as the Crow's Nest Pass railway was built. The hon. member for Edmonton will remember the stimulus that was given to the development of agriculture in Alberta when that was built. When that was accomplished the question of the development of a market for the farmers of Alberta had to be considered and at that time the smelting industry had almost failed. The farmers were badly in need of the market which would be afforded by the smelting industry and, when petitions were signed, not by manufacturers, I would have the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) understand, not signed by those gentlemen whom he speaks of, but signed by the farmers, the 'ranchers and the producers of the western plains, and when the late Government yielded to those petitions and gave that bounty on lead, it gave an added stimulus to agricultural development 322
in southern Alberta and afforded a ready and profitable market to the farmers there for their agricultural and dairy products. These are the facts in relation to that particular thing of which I have a personal knowledge. When the late Government gave a bonus or bounty to that industry, they provided that if the price of lead were at a certain figure it should not require any assistance, but if by reason of market conditions the world over the price of lead fell to a certain figure, then the bounty came automatically into effect. Five years went by and the two and a half million dollars were not expended, in 1908 the bounty was again renewed, and here we are again at the end of another five years. The Minister of Finance does not propose to grant the bounty in any event; he says: I propose to continue the principle that was inaugurated by the Liberals when in office, and it is a sound principle, that if by reason of conditions that are not local, but world-wide, the price of lead falls to a figure that would cause the industry to languish in the southern part of British Columbia; by this bounty I will stimulate that industry to the point of providing that lead shall have a certain price in the markets of the world, so that the industry may be maintained, giving employment to hundreds, nay thousands, of workmen throughout Kootenay, and thus the farmers of Alberta who are the ultimate beneficiaries, who produce the butter, the eggs, the meat, which supply the men in these smelters, and the oats which feed the horses, snail have a market, and in order that Canadians may in the end get the benefit of every dollar that is expended. It may well be that if after five years that industry does not languish, not one dollar of this money will be paid out. If on the other hand owing to changed economic conditions or the operation of the dumping propensities on the part of manufacturers in other parts of the world, the market for lead goes down below a certain figure, then this $600,000 would be available to assist that industry to be maintained on a profitable basis, and the people who profit most by it are not the lead manufacturers themselves, but the thousands of people who will be indirectly benefited. That is the reason I support this resolution.

When my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) sticks to the realm of imagination he is much better than when he dips into facts. As to the amount of butter and eggs supplied the Kootenay from Alberta, there was a time when there were few people in Alberta and many in the Kootenay, and then the Kootenay market amounted to a great deal to Alberta. But now-a-days there are many people in Alberta and fewer in the Kootenay, and the



market of the Kootenay is not of much value in that respect. My hon. friend has allowed his imagination to get mixed up with his facts.
Is it not a fact that a refrigerator goes each day into the Kootenay on the line of the Canadian Pacific railway?
I cannot say.
Well, I can, and that is the difference.
My hon. friend kqpws there are fewer people to-day in the Kootenay than last year, and fewer last year than the year before.

The men from the
Kootenay do not say so.

Nevertheless it is a fact. The number of people in the Kootenay 1 venture to say is no greater to-day than it was ten years ago when the smelter bounty was first given. There has been no increase in the population in the Kootenay which would bring about such a market for the farmers of Alberta as my hon. friend has suggested. The suggestion is absurd beyond words. The bounty was given for the benefit of the lead-mining industry, as everybody will admit, and in so far as it had an effect on that industry, it was desirable from the standpoint of the people of Alberta; but when my hon. friend rests his support of this proposal on the market, that the people of Alberta to-day find in the Kootenay because of the lead bounty, I can only say that he is drawing on his imagination. I suppose my hon. friend knows that the city of Calgary which he represents does not get from the surrounding country its own supplies of the articles that he says Alberta exports to Kootenay. The country around there does not produce sufficient of these articles to supply itself and yet the hon. gentleman says that he supports the lead bonus because it provides a market for the farmers of Alberta to which to export these products. The hon. gentleman should not take up the time of the House in talking such nonsense. His theory is fine, but the trouble about it is that it has no relation to the facts.
The only difference is that I say I know the facts, and the hon. gentleman says he does not know anythipg about them.
My hon. friend mentioned the price of oats, but does he know that three months ago oats in Alberta were cheaper than they were when this lead bounty was first given?

And yet my hon. friend
exhorts us to vote for this bounty because of the market it gives to the people of Alberta for their farm products, including oats.

What has that got to
do with it?

It has everything to do
with it. If the farmers of Alberta are not getting as good a market to-day after ten years of lead bounty, as they did before the lead bounty was put on, whatever the good will may have been the results are not to the benefit of the Alberta farmers. My hon. friend is off the track when he asks us to vote for this lead bounty in order to give a market to the farmers of Alberta.
Is the bounty on lead the only thing that affects the price of oats in Alberta?
Certainly not.
Then how do you apply your argument?

I am not applying any
argument; I am showing how ridiculous the application of the argument of the hon. member for Calgary is.
I said that the market was increased to the extent of the hundreds of men who were employed in these smelters.

There are no more men in Kootenay to-day than the day the lead bounty was first put on and they do not eat any more. Therefore there is no advantage to the Alberta farmers in the line my hon. friend has suggested.
I stated that the population at the smelters had increased.
Oh, yes.
And they are not producers of farm products, and therefore they have to rely on other people; among others, the farmers living in Alberta.

In the first place, the
farmers in southern Alberta, in the vicinity in which the hon. gentleman lives, have not any butter or eggs to send to Kootenay; they do not produce enough for the local wants.

Well, they are doing
it.

In the next place, so far as wheat and flour are concerned, we are raising so much wheat in Alberta that the market of Kootenay, if it was not there at all, would make no difference. And, so far as oats are concerned the price of oats is lower to-day than before the lead bounty was put on. I am dealing now with the state

of facts which the hon. member (Mr. Bennett) said induced him to support this bounty on lead. His theories were all right, but the facts were not there to support them. The general question of protection and free trade does not enter into the consideration of this lead bounty. We are brought back to the fact that the bounty on lead was given to help the lead industry to overcome a difficult period. It answered the purpose for which it was given and it is being renewed and re-established to-day by the present Government under conditions which did not exist when, it was first given; if such conditions had existed, it would never have been given. The hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Green) says: But the lead industry may be less prosperous later on; the price of lead may go down, and this sum of money should be in reserve to be paid out in case that should happen. I would say to the lead industry, and to the wheat industry, the cotton industry or any other industry: When you have had a fair chance to establish your business; when you have had the assistance of the people of Canada for a period of ten years to establish your business and to get on your feet, you must expect to carry your losses in the lean years out of your profits in the fat years, and you must not expect to play with the country a game of heads I win tails you lose. The people engaged in the lead industry have had their opportunity, and if they are unable to carry the fluctuations of the market to-day it is because the industry is not a good one and it is not worth while keeping it up.

I must apologize for troubling the committee again on this subject; but I should just like to say a word with regard to the argument which the hon. member'for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) has advanced with very great moderation and very great preciseness. As my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has pointed out, for the most part the market of Alberta is found in Calgary itself, but I may add that Calgary has grown, as a result of the independent and self-supporting agricultural enterprise of the province of Alberta, without the aid of protection at all; and that is the first answer I would make to my hon. friend from Calgary. While we in Alberta are very grateful and glad to avail ourselves of any market there is in British Columbia, it would be a mistake to attribute the prosperity of southern Alberta-and here I differ slightly from my hon. friend from Edmonton, because southern Alberta does export considerable agricultural produce to British Columbia-entirely to the lead, lumber and coal mining industries. These industries give us part of our market, but
this is where the argument of my hon. friend from Calgary halts. In accordance with the principles of justice and logic, if the people engaged in the lead enterprises in British Columbia are justified in coming to Alberta and saying to the farmers: We are giving you a market for your ag icultural products, tnerefore give us a bonus to help us to produce lead; clearly the farmers of Alberta would be equally justified in going to the lead people of British Columbia and saying: We are buying your lead products in Alberta, therefore give us a bonus on the production of beef and cattle. That is where the injustice is felt by the people of the plains and the whole of the consumers of Canada. I wish tc say that in reply to my hon. fiiend, and it is an argument that I am sure no hon. gentleman on tiie other side of the House can successfully meet.

That is precisely the attitude that has been taken by the farmers and a great many of the people .or many years in my part of the country and all through the province of British Columbia. The farmers of Alberta have a protection; there is a protective tariff on wheat, oats and beef. In a great many districts of British Columbia the people could have bought those products from the State of Washington cheaper than they could from the people of Alberta; yet I have rarely heard, the British Columbian farmers raise a voice against that condition, because they recognize the immense value to our province of keeping up interprovincial trade, even if they could not trade quite as economically with our own people, and of assisting in the endeavour to build up a united Canada. I think that position is absolutely fair.

I do not think the farmers of the plains consider that protection is of any service to them whatsoever, and I think they are better students of economic principles than the farmers Of British Columbia if the views of the latter are such as my hon. friend represents them to be. A protective tariff cannot be of any service in the production of a commodity, a large surplus of which is produced in any country, because the surplus going abroad, the price is regulated by the price in the-foreign market. I think that is an economic principle which no one has ever been able to overturn. I do not think the farmers of the plains get any benefit from protection; at any rate they do not believe they do, and they were very ready to part with that benefit, so far as the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were concerned, if I read aright the opinion of the people as shown by their votes in the general election of 1911. Again I would warn my hon. friend the Minister of Finance against giving too ready an ear to these
10191

infant industries, because my own study of this particular kind of industry that is always seeking protection is that it never reaches the period of adult life; it either remains an infant or it passes into decrepitude and old age. Hon. gentlemen opposite cannot talk of infant industries in Britain, but they represent the industries of that country as declining. That is always the cry of the protectionist; he is the emblem of human feebleness. He says: We have not grown up, and if you say: You are old enough to have grown up, he says: We have grown past adult life and are now in decrepitude and old age. I was much interested in reading a speech delivered in the United States House of Representatives not long ago, in the course of which the speaker gave one or two amusing illustrations with which I would like to deal for a moment, as I want to put my hon. friend on his guard against these healthy infants, who will be coming to him from time to time for assistance. The speaker said that these infant industries in the United States reminded him of the man who had an invalid and very cantankerous wife, and he prayed the Lord that he would restore her or do something with her. He also quoted a very familiar verse, but he altered the last line, and it is a common saying in the United States now:
Mary had a little lamb,
Its fleece was white as snow,
It followed her to Pittsburgh,
And look at the darned thing now.
We have our little lambs in Canada as well and they will follow my hon. friend to Toronto, but I do not want to see the darned things.

I wish to explain, as I said that I was going to move an amendment, and that the reason why I am not going to do so is that the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has since made a speech in which he has said that he is in favour of giving bounties at any rate at a certain stage of the game. That in causing the said letter to be sent to Senator Girroir, as above stated, the Minister of Public Works was guilty of an attempt unduly to influence the electors of the said electoral division and violated his duty ais a member of the Privy Council of Canada, as well as the rights and privileges of this House.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion I have the honour to make, may on its face appear to be of a partisan character. But, whilst a cursory reading of it might indicate that this is an attempt to strike at a political opponent, the matter I propose to

bring before the House is of serious importance and should receive the most careful consideration of all hon. members of this House -whether they sit on your right or on your left. It is a matter which affects the rights and privileges of the members of this House, a matter which is also calculated to reflect upon the honour of a member of the Privy Council of Canada, and of the Cabinet. It is a matter too which concerns the people, which concerns the whole people of Canada, for purity of elections and the free and independent expression of public opinion at the polls is a matter which not only every member of this House but every citizen of the country should guard most jealously. The case to which I call attention is not only an invasion of the rights and privileges of this House, not only shows conduct on the part of a Cabinet minister that is entirely at variance with parliamentary practice, but it goes further and, hard as the term may seem to be, it would indicate a violation of his oath of office on the part of a Privy Councillor. In addition to that it strikes at the ballot box and the purity of elections. You will remember that when the present Prime Minister of Canada issued his manifesto to the electorate, one of his strongest appeals was on the ground of purity in elections. I am not going to quote from that manifesto or give the argument he used on that occasion ; suffice it to say that we all recognize that in a country like this corruption and all attempts made to prevent the free and intelligent exercise of the franchise such as were made in the recent election in the county of Anti-gonish must be a matter of regret to all. This is a rather unpleasant duty I have to perform, but I feel it incumbent on me because the constituency I have the honour to represent has received undue prominence in connection with the circumstances which I shall relate. The county of Antigonish has hitherto had the reputation of being one of the purest and most incorruptible in Canada. We have always boasted of the fact that the people of that county tried to exercise the franchise independently and conscientiously and according to their lights. For the first time in the history of Antigonish county, so far as I know the attempt has been made to buy up the electors in platoons. It is proper that I should on this occasion resent the insult cast upon the people of Antigonish, Conservative and Liberal, by the attempt of the Minister of Public Works to bribe the electors e* that county in platoons as he and his minions sought to do in that election. I	should very much	preferthat	the task	of bringing	these
matters to the attention of the House were imposed on someone else. But, for the reason I have already given, I
consider it my duty to bring the matter to the attention of the House and in doing so I feel that I shall have the endorsation not only of the Liberals of Antigonish county, but of the Conservatives as well, for if there is one thing that we down there pride ourselves on it is that as far as elections are concerned, we have never been amenable to the corrupt practices used in some parts of the country, particularly where the Minister of Public Works has been operating in the conduct of elections. Antigonish is neither corrupt nor corruptible. It is true that perhaps in sections of that county as in other places there are men who may be influenced by promises such as were made by Senator Girroir representing, as he said, the Government on this occasion. But let me say that these men, one and all, would spurn a direct bribe or money offered for their votes. It is, after all, a comparatively small matter who represents the constitu ency, but it is a matter of the greatest im portance that the purity, honesty and inde pendence of the electorate be maintained and its good reputation preserved. Therefore, it is my duty to ventilate these matters before the House.
May I explain the conditions which led to the by-election of the 16th of January, 1913? A vacancy occurred in the local legislature by the appointment to the Senate of Senator Girroir, then a member of the Legislative Assembly of Nova Scotia, representing the constituency which I have the honour to represent. While we in Antigonish county are proud of his appointment and appreciate the fact that he comes from Antigonish county, the honour is not an honour to that county in particular. It so happened that there was a vacancy in the French Acadian representation in the Senate from Nova Scotia owing to the death of the late Senator Comeau, and as Senator Girroir possessed all the qualifications necessary for the position of senator, being a good representative of the French Aca-dians in that province, than whom there are no more intelligent, industrious, thrifty and upright people in Canada, we were proud to see his appointment to represent that large body who were well worthy of the representation they received. Whilst the French Acadians may well be proud of their representative, they owe no particular gratitude to this Government for the appointment made on this occasion, as they had a right to have one of their members appointed to the Senate owing to the precedent established by the late Liberal Administration.
If any particular credit is to be given for the appointment of a French Acadian representative in the red chamber, it is due to the late Laurier Government that for the first time the province of Nova Scotia recognized that body in the appointment of the late lamented Senator Comeau.
The vacancy caused by the death of

Senator Comeau was filled by the appointment of Mr. Girroir and the local election came on. The Conservative party seemed to attach a great deal of importance to the issue in that constituency. Perhaps it was due to the fact that the naval question was then an issue, and in Antigonish there is only one opinion on that question; the electors are dead opposed to the policy of the present Government. On that account I suppose the Government felt it necessary to put forward some herculean effort in order that they might hold their own in that constituency. Be it noted that the county was represented in the Legislature by a Liberal and a Conservative. The Conservative candidate who went into the general election in June, 1911, was elected by a majority of two hundred and twenty-nine. In the by-eleotion of January the 16th the Conservative candidate was elected by two hundred and ninety-eight. The Conservative candidate in 1913 got fifty-five more votes than the Conservative candidate in 1911, while the Liberal got fourteen votes less in 1913 than in 1911. Thus -the result did not amount to very much so far as any political gain or advantage went. The election was held on the 16th day of January. On the 9th day of January, one week before the election, there ap peared in the local paper the item to which I shall presently refer. There is only one paper published in the constituency, a weekly religious, Catholic organ, non-partisan in politics. It is a paper very highly .respected by all classes of people and it is exceedingly careful in -the publication of news. It is not of the sensational type, it has none of the yellow journal qualities that we see in many other papers. When a news item appears in that paper it is taken as correct. There appeared in that paper what, to ninety-nine per cent of the people would appear to be a news item, but which was in reality an advertisement. It was a letter purporting to come from the office of the Minister of Public Works. The letter as it appeared in the Casket of January 9th, 1913, read:
Office of the Minister of Public Works of Canada.
Senator Girroir:
Ottawa December 28, 1912.
My Dear Sir,-Your letter of the 24th instant addressed to the Minister of Public Works received, and, in accordance with your request, I am enclosing you herewith a list of the items which have been placed in the supplementary estimates for Antigonish county for 1913-14.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) George Buskard,
Minister's Secretary.
To E. L. Girroir, Esq.,
Barrister, Antigonish, N.S.
Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
That letter when received in the constituency caused a great deal of -comment. It stated distinctly that the secretary was enclosing herewith a list of the items placed in the supplementary estimates for Antigonish for 1913-14, and it stated that the letter was sent to Senator Girroir in accordance with his request. I have not Senator Girroir's letter to the Minister of Public Works, but there can be no question about the contents of that letter, for the letter which the minister's secretary writes on December 28 says distinctly that it is in accordance with the request of Senator Girroir that he is furnishing a list of the items which have been placed in the supplementary estimates fo-r Antigonish county for the years 1913-14. There is no suggestion that this is a list of items to which the senator had called attention on various occasions or of items noted for consideration on the preparation of the estimates, supplementary or main. Mark you, -Mir. Speaker, at that time neither the main nor the supplementary estimates had been prepared, although the letter would suggest otherwise. The tmain estimates were not brought down for nearly two months after that -and -the supplementary estimates are not down yet; but still the secretary of the minister, on the eve of an election, writes this letter to one of his henchmen, in which he states that he is sending a list of the items which have been placed in the supplementary estimates for that county. I have read the letter. The enclosure as it appeared in the Gasket was as follows:-

Thus read the letter and enclosure which purported to come from the Minister of Public Works, and which was inserted in the Antigonish Casket of January 9. It is a weekly paper, as I have said, and there was no other issue until election day. It happens to be published on Thursday, and the election was on the following Thursday, the 16th, so that there was no opportunity of contradicting those estimates in the paper which disseminated them throughout the county. I had seen the original letter a few evenings before the date on which the estimates appeared in the Antigonish Casket, and I was amazed to find that it was signed by Mr. Buskard, secretary of the Minister of Public Works. I thought perhaps it was intended to be used secretly in the campaign at the suggestion of the Minister of Public Works, for we know that he prides himself on the fact that he knows how to win elections. I thought that perhaps this was one of the methods which he intended to be used in te dark, but I did not think that 'the letter and the enclosure would be made public. To my amazement, however, they did appear in the Casket newspaper just as I have read them. When I read the letter in the Casket, notwithstanding the fact that it purported to be signed by Mr. BuskaTd, I had some doubts as to its authenticity, and when I came to Ottawa I made inquiries of the minister, and put a question on the Order Paper. I quoted the letter as it appeared in the Casket, and put the following question :
2.	Did the Minister of Public Works or his secretary send, or authorize to be sent, to Senator Girroir, of Antigonish, N.S., the said
letter and inclosure?
3.	If not, did the minister or his secretary send, or authorize to be sent, any letter to Senator Girroir in the month of December last, respecting the estimates, or proposed expenditure for Antigonish ?
4.	If so, what was such letter and enclosure ?
You would suppose Mr. Speaker that a categorical answer would be given to these questions. There was nothing ambiguous about the language; they were plain simple questions. But what answer did the minister give? He replied as follows:
Mr. R gers: The Minister of Public Works had no knowledge whatever respecting the matter referred to. Senator Girroir, who from time to time had interested himself in making requests that certain work at different points should be carried on during the coming year, asked to be supplied with a memorandum of the applications which he had so named, in answer to which request the following is a correct copy of the memorandum sent:
You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Public Works evaded the questions that were put to him. He said he had no knowledge whatever respecting the matter referred to, and in the next breath he turned around and said that the Senator had been inquiring about certain works which he wished to be carried on at various points during the coming year, and that he had asked to be supplied with a memorandum. But you will observe that the letter sent by the secretary of the minister is not consistent with any suggestion of that kind. It is as clear and explicit as it could be and states:
I am enclosing you herewith a list of the items which have been placed in the supplementary estimates.
He does not say that he is sending a list of items to which his attention had been called by Senator Girroir. The very idea that such a list was necessary is absurd. Senator Girroir's memory is not so short that he required a list of the items from the minister. Senator Girroir had those things as pat in his memory as I have had them all along. I had written to the Department of Public Works sending a list of the various items which required attention, and I could recite them without any difficulty, morning, noon and night, and Senator Girroir could do the same. Therefore, whilst under the rules of debate we have to accept the statement of the Minister of Public Works, I leave it to the House to say whether the answers he gave to my questions were honest and frank, or consistent with the truth in any shape or form. Let me direct your attention again, Mr. Speaker, to his answer. He says that the Senator had asked to be supplied with a memorandum of the applications for appropriations which the latter had made, and that in answer to that request the memorandum had been sent. Let me call your attention to the list which the minister says was sent to Senator Girroir, and let me ask you, Mr. Speaker, and the House, to institute a comparison between the list or enclosure sent to the senator, according to the minister, and the list which was published in the Casket. On page 2440 of 'Hansard,' January 29, 1913, it is stated that the list sent to the senator was as follows:
List of amounts for Antigonish county, Nova Scotia, noted for estimates, 1913-11. Main Estimates.
Then followed the items just as they apeared in the Casket with one exception: ' Blue Bock, $8,200,' as it appeared in the newspaper instead of $1,200, as it appears in the minister's answer. You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that in the letter which appeared in the Casket on the eve of the elec-

tion there was no heading such as is found in the memorandum which the minister brought down. Any reader of the Casket would come to the conclusion that the min ister was sending Senator Girroir a list of the items which had been placed in the estimates, and not a list which had been merely noted for the main -or supplementary estimates. Let me again remind you of the fact that at that time the main estimates had not been prepared. A few days before he House rose for Christmas recess I took occasion to go to the Public Works Department to call their attention to some works which were of pressing need, and while I was there I was told that the estimates had not yet been prepared but that they would be considered during the holidays. When this letter was read by Senator Girroir at a joint meeting at which we were both present, about the 6th or 7th January, I took occasion to call attention to the fact that the estimates had not yet been prepared and that the letter of Mr. Buskard, if it were genuine, contained statements that were absolutely untrue. The answer that was made to that was that the letter came from the Department of Public Works and it was there to speak for itself. Let me emphazize the fact that there is a difference between the memorandum which was isent to Senator Girroir according to the minister and the same as it appeared in the Antigonish Casket. In the first place the letter in the Antigonish Casket does not state that the list is a list of items noted for the estimates for 1913-14. The head note after enclosure or memorandum is absent. In the letter which appeared in the Antigonish Casket it is stated, in addition to what is contained in the memorandum as-brought- down by the minister that:
There will also be placed in the general vote for dredging amounts for Lakevale and Bayfield; and an amount for repair of old wharf
at Georgeville will be placed in estimates when exact amount of damage is ascertained.
In the memorandum which was brought down by the minister that language is not found. The publication in the Casket -contained a suppression of the head note and an addition at the end of the enclosure sent the senator. When I read the reply of the minister to my question I was very much surprised. I could not understand how it was that such statements could have been made publicly by -Senator Girroir during the election campaign, and that such a letter should be found in the Casket. I found, as I have said, that there was a variation as between the memorandum which the minister says he sent to Senator Girroir and the letter which Senator Girroir had published. I would like to direct the attention of the House to the definition of Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
forgery as found in the Criminal Code, section 422:
Forgery is the making of a false document knowing it to be false, with the intention that it shall in any way be used or acted upon as genuine, to the prejudice of anyone whether within Canada or not, or that some person should he induced, by the belief that it is genuine, to do or refrain from doing anything, whether within Canada or not.
2.	Making a false document includes altering a genuine document in any material part, and making any material addition to it, &c.
3.	Forgery is complete as soon as the document is made with such knowledge and intent as aforesaid, but though the offender may not have intended that any particular person should use or act upon it as genuine, &c.
While I do not say that the alteration of the letter which came from the hon. Minister of Public Works by the elimination of the heading from it, namely, ' List of items for Antigonish county noted for estimates, 1913-14/ and whilst I do not say that the addition of the words to the enclosure referred to in the letter as it appeared in the Casket, and which were not found in the letter sent by the Minister of Public Works to Senator Girroir, according to the statement of the Minister of Public Works, constitute a forgery, yet I say it comes pretty near to it and there can be no denying the fact that the senator, by the alteration of the original letter and the addition made to it, published a garbled document for the purpose of influencing the electors. If the enclosure had been published as the Minister of Public Works says he supplied it to the senator, it would not have had the same effect because the electorate would have seen that it was only a list of items that had been noted for the estimates for Antigonish county. But these words were left out so that the people were led to believe that the senator had authority to pledge the minister that these works would be provided for. When the minister gave his answer on the 29th January, he rather evaded the question that was put to him, as I have already pointed out. He did not give a straight -categorical answer to the question. On that occasion I tried to get the minister to answer -the question fully. I said:
The question as to whether the minister or his secretary sent or authorized to he sent the letter referred to has been evaded.
The minister replied:
The Minister of Public Works did not authorize or send any such letter. I understand that the words ' or his secretary ' appear in the question, but I did not know they had any hearing upon the matter.
He said that he did not know that the words ' or his secretary ' had any bearing
MAT? 19, 1913
upon the matter. He was not frank in making that statement. The question that was asked was:
Did the Minister of Public Works or his secretary send, or authorize to be sent, to Senator Girroir, of Antigonish, N.S., the said letter and enclosure?
The letter is signed by his secretary. Surely, it would have occurred to the minister that the question as to whether his secretary sent that letter would have an important bearing on the matter. It looks very much like the old case of where a man's conscience is not at ease he is apt to say and do things that under other circumstances he would not say or do. He evaded that question and he sought to create the impression that he was not responsible for the letter.
I followed the thing up a little further. On February 3, I referred to the same letter as it had appeared in the Antigonish Casket and which gave a list of the items. I asked the following question:
Did the secretary of the Minister of Public Works send, or authorize to send, to Senator Girroir, of Antigonish, N.S., the 9aid letter and enclosure?
You will remember that when I asked the question on January 29, the minister evaded it to a certain extent. On February 3, he stated that:
The following letter and memorandum were sent by the secretary of the Minister of Public Works.
The letter and memorandum are given at page 2691 of ' Hansard.' They are set out in the resolution which I have submitted for the consideration of the House. What has the minister to say for himself in connection with the publication of estimates in advance of their submission to this House? It was a violation of the rights and privileges of this House to publish estimates in advance and I could quote authority for that statement from May and other writers on parliamentary procedure. I do not propose to quote authorities in detail, but I would refer the House to page 74 of May, where there will be found the following:
It is declared to be a breach of privilege for a member, or any other person, to publish the evidence taken before a select committee, until it has been reported to the House;
In 1911 a statement purporting to represent proposals contained in confidential papers referred to the select committee on the civil-list with a report of the proceedings of the committee was published in a newspaper.
This was deemed to be a breach of privilege. Then, at page 416, it is stated that:
No member, or any other person, may ublish any portion of the evidence taken y or documents presented to select committees, which have not been reported to the House; and this rule extends equally to the
report of a committee before it has been presented to the House.
I shall not weary the House by quoting authorities to the effect that in so far as these estimates are concerned, it is the right and privilege of the House to first receive the estimates before they are submitted to the public. The letter which purported to have been sent by the minister through his secretary contained statements that were absolutely false because the estimates were not prepared at the date the letter was sent. The main estimates were not prepared then and the supplementary estimates have not been prepared yet. In addition to that, the minister, through his secretary, in _ sending that letter which was false on its face, violated his duty, and he was guilty of improper conduct, both as a minister and a privy councillor, in giving out information of that kind. I go so far as to say that the minister had no right to disclose what had been noted in the supplementary estimates in this manner. If I want to find what items there are for Antigonish county in the supplementary estimates and I ask the engineer in the department. I am politely told that inlormation cannot be given. We have had numerous incidents in this House of hon. gentlemen inquiring whether certain works were provided for in the supplementary estimates, and the invariable answer was given that the estimates had not yet been brought down. The Prime Minister himself a few days ago stated that it was not proper that information of that kind should be given until it was imparted to Parliament in the regular way. The effect of the answers to the question put to the minister, as found in ' Hansard ' of February 3, 1913, and January 29, 1913, is to place Senator Girroir in the position of having garbled the letter sent to him. While I know Senator Girroir to be an extreme partisan, and one who is prepared to fight the game to a finish, I do not believe he would be guilty of what inspirit if not in letter would appear to be forgery, and take the risk of the penalty prescribed for that offence. I took the precaution of ascertaining who sent that letter to the Casket newspaper, and I ascertained it was Senator Girroir who brought the letter of the minister with the enclosure to the newspaper office, which published both in good faith. Ninety-nine out of one hundred people would believe this was a matter of news. It was published however as an advertisement and paid for at so much per inch. The Casket newspaper was imposed upon most shamefully.

speechtext:
I did not say there
was forgery in law; I said there was something akin to forgery and I Tead the definition of forgery. In the letter which the Senator had published in the Antigonish Casket, a list of items was given as I have read them here, without any head note, and in the letter which the minister states he sent to Senator Girroir there was this head note:
List of amounts for Antigonish county, Nova Scotia, noted for estimates 1913-14.

Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
