speechtext: Will you state on your responsibility as a member of this House that you did not see the letter sent to Senator Girroir in which the words were plainly set out as the minister stated?

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend puts a straight question and I give a straight answer. I did see that letter and I saw that these words were there and I commented upon them, and I directed the attention of the audience to the fact that this letter was simply a list of items which had been noted and not a list of items which had been placed in the estimates. To this the Senator replied: there is the letter and the letter says expressly, I am enclosing you herewith a list of the items which have been placed in the supplementary estimates for Antigonish county for 1913-14; and the senator addressing the audience said:	All the ingenuity of my
learned friend cannot get away from the fact that here is a letter signed by the minister's secretary in which it is expressly stated that these items have been placed in the supplementary estimates. That was the argument of Senator Girroir, and that is why whe.n I returned to the House after the holidays I put the question to the minister, setting forth the letter as it appeared in the Casket to ascertain juste what had been sent to the senator. I confess I was exceedingly surprised when I read in the Casket that this heading was omitted. I was also equally surprised to find that there was added to the letter which appeared in the Casket the words:
There will also be placed in the general vote for the dredging amounts for Lakevale and Bayfield, and an amount for repair for old wharf at Georgeville, will be placed in estimates when exact amount of damage is ascertained.
That was the letter which the senator published in the newspaper. I direct attention to the fact that the minister says he did not send that letter. I suppose his answer will be that his secretary sent it. Every hon. gentleman in this House knows that a large percentage of the letters whith the minister sends to hon. gentlemen are signed by his private secretary, and let. me say that this letter purports to have been written with the authority of the minister. This was not a letter which was addressed to the secretary of the minister and to which he replied; it was a letter which had been addressed to the minister himself for the letter reads:
Your letter of the 24th instant addressed to the Minister of Public Works received, and in accordance with your request, I am enclosing you herewith a list of the items which Have been placed in the supplementary estimates for Antigonish county for 1913-14.
The secretary purports to speak for the minister; in his capacity as secretary he

answers a letter addressed to his minister, and that answer binds the minister. It would be impossible properly to conduct the business of any department of the Government unless the secretary to the head of the department were responsible to the minister for his actions. In the oath of office taken by every private secretary, which hon. gentlemen of this House can find in the Civil Service Act, the secretary swears that he will properly conduct himself in the position to which he is appointed. It will not lie in the mouth of the minister, therefore, to say that he did not write the letter, and that it was written by his secretary without his authority. If the secretary had no authority for writing the letter, why does he still occupy his position? Why was he not instantly dismissed from office? Every hon. gentleman knows that any private secretary who flagrantly violated the rules of his office would not hold his position for an hour. The very fact that the minister has retained the services of his secretary shows that he assumes responsibility for what the secretary wrote. If that is the case, the minister, through his secretary, wrote a letter which was false, and which gave information which was entirely at variance with the facts. I have said that a minister of the Crown is not at liberty to disclose what takes place in Council, or to publish in advance any estimates which he has under consideration. Let me quote from Dodd on Dignities, Privileges and Precedence, page 26. Speaking of the Cabinet Council, the writer says:
As they are more immediately responsible for the conduct of public affairs, their deliberations are always considered confidential and kept secret, even from their colleagues who are less exalted in office.
Their deliberations have to be kept secret from their colleagues, and neither the hon. the Minister of Public Works nor any other minister of the Crown is at liberty to leave the Council Chamber and tell any one of his supporters that any particular item is to be provided for in the estimates when they are brought down. In Thom's Book of the Court, page 230, it is stated that:
The duty of a Privy Councillor appears from the oath which he takes on his admission to the office to be:
1.	To advise the King according to the best of his cunning and discretion.
2.	To advise the King's honour, and the good of the public, without partiality, through affection, love, need, doubt or dread.
3.	To keep the King's Counsel secret.
4.	To avoid corruption.
5.	To help and strengthen what shall be resolved in the Council.
6.	To withstand all persons who would attempt the contrary.
7.	To observe, keep and do all that a good and true Counsellor ought to , do to his Sovereign Lord.
The Cabinet is a committee of the Privy Council.
These are the duties of a Privy Councillor, and, as hon. gentlemen know, the Cabinet is only a committee of the Privy Council. Let me read to you the oath taken by a Privy Councillor when he assumes office:
You	do solemnly
promise and swear that you will serve His Majesty truly and faithfully in the place of His Council in this His Majesty's Dominion of Canada, you will keep close and secret all such matters as shall be treated, debated and resolved on in Privy Council, without publishing or disclosing the same or any part thereof, by word, writing, or any otherwise to any person out of the same Council, but to such only as be of the Council, and yet of any matter so propounded, treated and debated in any such Privy Council, shall touch any particular person, sworn of the same council upon any such matter as shall in any wise concern his loyalty and fidelity to the King's Majesty, you will in no wise open the same to him, but keep it secret, as you would from any person, until the King's Majesty's pleasure be known in that behalf. You will in all things to be moved, treated and debated in any such Privy Council, faithfully, honestly and truly declare your mind and opinion to the honour and benefit of the King's Majesty, and the good of his subjects without partiality or exception of persons, in no wise forebearing so to do from any manner of respect, favour, love, meed, displeasure, or dread of any person or persons whatsoever. In general you will be vigilant, diligent and circumspect in all your doings touching the King's Majesty's affairs; All which matters and things you will faithfully observe and keep, as a good councillor ought to do to the utmost of your power, will and discretion. So help you God.
It is evident that the statement in the minister's letter is false, for on February 19 of this year the supplementary estimates had not been considered. On that day, after quoting the letter to Senator Girroir and the enclosures, I asked the minister -the following questions:
Have the items mentioned under the head-, ing supplementary estimates, or any of them, been placed in the supplementary estimates for Antigonish county, for 1913-14, as stated in said letter? If not, is it the intention of the Government to place these items in the supplementary estimates this year?
The Minister of Public Works made the following answer:
The supplementary estimates have not yet been considered.
Some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House about three weeks ago asked further questions with regard to the supplementary estimates, and the minister replied that they had not been considered, so that the minister could not have been in a position to give any information with regard to them even at that late date, although through his secretary, he said in

his letter to Senator Girroir live months ago that he was enclosing a list of the items which had been placed in the supplementary estimates for Antigonish county. As far as the main estimates were concerned, if these items had been considered in council, before he wrote the senator, I submit that the Minister of Public Works should not have given out that information. I shall not comment further upon the oath of office taken by the minister and the necessity for absolute secrecy in that regard. The minister will doubtless try to place the responsibility upon his secretary, as he has done on other occasions. We had such an experience in connection with the Donaldson case; a steal was perpetrated upon this country and the minister attempted to place the blame upon his secretary. Certain correspondence that was brought down contained the initials ' G. B.'-George Buskard -and the minister endeavoured to escape responsibility by placing the blame upon his secretary. I think, however, that such an argument will not go very far with the people.
The works referred to are necessary in the county of Antigonish, and it was perfectly proper that they should have been provided for. Provision should now be made for these works in the estimates for the present year if justice and fair play be meted out to the county of Antigonish If some of these items had appeared in the estimates the year before last as they should, they would not bulk so large on the present occasion. The greater portion of these items were provided for by the late Administration, but the present Government cut them out of the estimates they brought down, and refused to do anything for the country until the local by-election was held. It is quite true that these items amount to a large sum in bulk even without taking into consideration the dredging and other repairs referred to in that letter. These supplementary estimates alone amount to $195,000- $16 for every man, woman and child in the county, or $81 for every vote polled in the election. It is true these sums bulk large. But, as I have pointed out, if those had been voted and expended last year or the year before as they should have been, the vote would not have bulked so large in the estimates of this year. But that is not the question; you should not consider what it amounts to for each individual, what you should consider is:	Are these works
necessary and proper? I submit that these works should be built. Let me ask the minister then, that when the estimates are brought down every one of these items will be found there and that the money will be spent. It is right and proper that the money should be voted and spent. He Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
owes that to the people; he owes it to himself; he owes it to the reputation of Senator Girroir. It is true that the Conservatives workers in that county had to drink a cup of humiliation that was filled to the brim. If the Minister of Public Works wishes to give an antidote to the political poison these people had to drink, he will see to it that all those items are provided for in the estimates.
Now, I come to another question of that election, which at first blush may not seem directly relevant to the motion, but as I proceed you will see that it is pertinent. It involves the conduct of the Prime Minister in seeking to influence the electors on that occasion. The Minister of Public Works is not the only guilty party. I claim that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways lent themselves to a scheme to mislead and deceive the farmers of Antigonish county for the purpose of unfairly influencing that election. Last year, weather conditions were so unfavourable that there was a considerable shortage of hay in that constituency. In some sections the crop was not more than one-third of the average. The year before also the hay crop had been light. On the 4th of September, the Farmers' Association of Antigonish county, after due consideration, passed a resolution memorialising the Government for free transportation of hay over the Intercolonial railway. I shall not dwell on the facts that justify their action, nor refer to precedents that could be invoked in support of their request. Suffice it to say that they were encouraged in this matter by Senator Girroir, who volunteered to lend them his assistance and led them to hope that they would secure what they desired. Finding that nothing was done, or that nothing seemed to have been done by the senator in this regard when the House met, at the request of some of the members of the association, I called on the Minister of Railways and Canals to ascertain whether or not free transportation would be provided. I was informed that the Railway Department knew nothing at all about the matter. In the ordinary course one would suspect that the request made would be submitted to the officers of the department for investigation. I was surprised that they had heard nothing about it, so I hied myself to the Minister of Agriculture, who informed me that he had received such a petition which he forwarded to the Minister of Railways and in a general way he discussed the matter. I called on the Minister of Railways, and he informed me he did not see how the Intercolonial railway could give free transportation. He very kindly discussed the subject from

his point of view, but held out no hope of free transportation. I called his attention to the fact that the farmers of Antigonish desired to know at as early a day as possible what the position o'f the Minister of Railways was in this matter as they would have to make other arrangement if the request they had made of him was not granted. H.e told me that in a day or two he would give his decision, and that in the meantime he would need to consult the Prime Minister. The day or two passed, and other days passed, and I received no reply; so on the 26th of November, I put questions on the Order Paper as follows:
1.	Is it the intention of the Railway Depart-1 meat to allow free transportation of hay over) the Intercolonial railway from the province^ of Quebec to the eastern counties of Nova' Scotia, or any of them?
2.	What relief, if any, in the matter ofl freight rates on hay to be carried over the Intercolonial railway for the farmers of the eastern counties of Nova Scotia is proposed?
That question ought to have been very easily answered; the Minister of Railways ought to have been able to state what the position of the department was. But every time that question was called until after the by-election in Antigonish the Prime Minister rose in his place and said 'stand'. And on the 12th of December he told me: The matter is under consideration. Now, I want to say that the Prime Minister was not candid, he was not honest in making such -a statement, because, as a matter of fact, the Minister of Railways had decided as early as the 14th of October that free transportation should not be granted. I have here the papers brought down on the 8th o!f March pursuant to an order of this House on my motion for:
A copy of all petitions, resolutions, letters, telegrams and the correspondence, relating to free or reduced transportation of hay over the Intercolonial railway for the farmers of Antigonish county.
In this connection, let me say that while this return purports t-o cover all the papers and correspondence on this subject, I cannot find a line from Antigonish, I cannot find the resolution of the Farmers' Association or any letter or telegram or any intimation of any kind made to any of the departments of this Government on the pant of the farmers of Antigonish county. I find representation from Cape Breton, from Inverness, from Richmond and from Gysiborough but .not from Antigonish. Reverting to what I was about to say, I find here the following letter from Mr. Thos. Gallant, of Inverness, who has the patronage for Inverness county:
Inverness, N.S., Oct. 9, 1912. Hon. Frank Cochrane,
Minister of Railways,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir,-The shortage of the hay crop in this county places the farmers in a very precarious condition. It will be necessary for them to import a very considerable quantity of hay. I would recommend that this hay be transported over the Intercolonial railway free of charge. This would be a great help to the farmers of this county, and I would respectfully ask for your favourable consideration of this matter.
Yours sincerely,
Thos. Gallant.
And what do you suppose was the answer? It was as follows:
19th Oct., 1912.
Dear Sir,-I have yours of October 9 asking that the Intercolonial railway should transport hay free for the farmers along the line whose hay crop has failed. While I sympathize with the farmers, I do not see how the Intercolonial railway can he expected to do this.
Yours very truly,
F. Cochrane.
Thomas Gallant, Esq.,
Inverness, N.S.
There is no mistaking that answer. The Minister of Railways was frank, honest and aboveboard and told the people he could not see his way to grant the free transportation. I find also the following letter:
_	November 9, 1912.
Dear Sirs,-I have yours of November 7, and in reply may say that it is not intended to carry hay via Intercolonial railway free of charge from Quebec to Nova Scotia. This could only he done by a grant which would cover freight charges, as the road must pay its fixed charges.
Yours truly,
F. Cochrane.
Messrs. S. R. Griffin & Sons,
Goldboro,
Guysborough county, N.S.
The request was for the carriage of hay into Nova Scotia, and not for the carriage of hay from some particular section of that province. The Prime Minister refused to answer the question that was put to him although his Minister of Railways had decided long before that that there would be no free transportation. Why did he suppress the information that I had a right to obtain from him? I had a perfect right to ask those questions on behalf of mv constituents and to receive an answer. Was it for the purpose of influencing the election there that the Government maintained such golden silence. There could be no other reason. What would you think of a Prime Minister of this country, the leader of a great party, who would stoop so low as to take advantage of the farmers of Antigonish or any other county in the

province of Nova Scotia in order, forsooth, that he might win a by-election. The situation might have been very serious to the farmers of eastern Nova Scotia. Suppose the price of hay had gone up in December, that it had risen from week to week and from month to month, and the farmers had had to pay 25 per cent or 50 per cent or 75 per cent more for the hay in the middle of the winter than they had to pay in the fall or the early part of the season. In that case the farmers would have suffered. It is true that the price did not go up but for that no thanks are due to the minister or to any of his colleagues or to this Government. I say that it was the lowest of petty, picayune politics on the part of the Primt Minister, to use such a trivial matter to influence the electors.
Let me refer to the minister's statement at page 1786 of the unrevised ' Hansard,' made a few days after the election in Antigonish. The hon. member for Richmond county asked a question about free transportation of hay over the Intercolonial, and then the Minister of Railways replied. He had no difficulty about speaking after the election. He and the Premier were as mute as oysters until after the day of the by-election, but immediately after it the minister said, in reply to the question of the hon. member for Richmond:
I have taken the attitude all along that if anything is done in that respect it should be done by special vote not by Order in Council.
You have heard that the minister states: I have taken the attitude all along. He had not come to this conclusion recently, he had taken that attitude from the very inception of the request that there should be no free transportation. Why did not the Minister of Railways frankly state that on the 26th of November? This question ot the free transportation of hay was used in the by-election for all it was worth. There was not a Conservative speaker from one end of the county to the other who did not picture the benevolence, the generosity of this Government in going to give the farmers free transportation. There was not a district in the county in which the appeal was not made that the farmers should show their appreciation of what the Conservative party at Ottawa was doing for them in the matter of free transportation of hay. They should therefore vote for the Conservative candidate.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Will the hon. member, on his responsibility as a member of this House, say that the statement was ever made in that county that the Government would provide free transportation of hay?

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Well, well, well, I am surprised that my hon. friend should ask Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
such a question. Shall I have to read the requests that were made-

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Answer the question.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Certainly. The request in Antigonish was for free transportation over the Intercolonial. That was the resolution passed on the 4th of September.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: But we want the promise of the Government, the statement made by Government supporters. I am quite prepared to admit that the request was made.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I think I shall be able to convince my hon. friend that he has not even that loop-hole of escape. If he thinks that possibly by some hair splitting distinction, by juggling with words, he can put that construction on it I am quite content that he should do it, but I say on my responsibility that the farmers of' Antigonish and the people of Antigonish understood the proposition before the Government to be free transportation over the Intercolonial for their hay, as was granted in 1904.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I think the hon. member is quibbling between Government and Intercolonial. See if that is what is bothering him.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Possibly, but the people of Antigonish understood it.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I heard it and before I have finished I shall produce the evidence. Let me read the advertisement which appeared in the Casket of January 9, two days before the election.
Arrangements have been made for fjree transportation of hay into this county for farmers only. Persons desiring hay can leave their orders with C. Edgar Whidden from whom full information can be obtained. The following persons have been appointed a committee to oversee the matter:
A. D. Chisholm.
P. S. Floyd.
Dan. D. McDonald.
This appeared in the Antigonish Casket on January 9.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Absolutely true.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
iviy hon. friend has a happy faculty of finding rest when he is in an uncomfortable position. What was the request of the farmers? It was free transportation of hay over the Intercolonial by the Intercolonial. They never expected that Senator Girroir or the Conservative organization or the boodle fund of the Tory party, if they have such a thing, were to be appealed to for the purpose of paying for the transportation of the hay of the farmers in the county of Antigonish, they would pay for the transportation of their

own hay rather than nave somebody else pay it; but they felt as they were large contributors to the exchequer of the Intercolonial, as the Intercolonial was reaping a large profit and benefit from them and through them, that they were not ashamed to' ask the Intercolonial to help them out on this particular occasion and carry their hay free. They did not ask the Conservative party of Canada or the Conservative organization of Antigonish or anybody else to pay for the transportation of their hay. This letter appeared in the Casket of January 9. People were surprised. This man Floyd was a Liberal, a very respectable man in the county of Antigonish, one of the most respectable citizens of the county. I shall not say anything about the other gentlemen, they are both very strong Conservatives.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Did he vote Liberal
last year?

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I do not know, I am not supposed to know how he voted. I would call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that there is not very much room for jubilation and glorification over the victory in Antigonish when you come to consider the base, despicable and ignoble methods resorted to. There is little comfort for the Conservatives in the fact that the Liberal candidate had only fourteen votes less than he had in the general election a year and a half or two years before and the Conservative candidate had fifty-five votes more. Considering the Herculean efforts they made to win that constituency, they have not very much to glory over. I was going to refer to those gentlemen who signed this notice respecting the free transportation of hay. Mr. Floyd was approached and asked what the arrangement was, and he at once said: I know nothing at all about any arrangement for the free transportation of hay; I have not heard of any such arrangement with the Intercolonial railway or with anybody else; the first time I knew about it was when I read it in the Casket. So he repudiated it at once. The Secretary of the Farmers' Association sent a telegram to Mr. Tiffin, the traffic manager of the Intercolonial railway:
To E. Tiffin,
Antigonish, Jan. 11, 1913,
Traffic Manager, Intercolonial railway. Moncton.
Wire collect what arrangements made regarding transportation of hay for this county. Rush.
Alexander McDonald, Secretary Farmers' Association.
That same evening came the reply:
To Alexander McDonald,
Secretary Farmers' Association, Antigonish.
Your wire this date. I am not aware of any
special arrangements in regard to transportation of hay for Antigonish county.
E. Tiffin,
The Conservatives had the notice in the paper, and the farmers were led to believe that there was to be free transportation. The traffic manager was wired, and he replied that he was not aware of any such arrangement. But that did not stop the Conservatives. They said: Oh, Tiffin does not know anything about it; he is not the man who has to do with this thing. Sc they issued a circular immediately to the electors of Antigonish in which they said:
: The Halifax Morning Chronicle also is being freely circulated with farther sensational statements about hay, &c. Mr. Whidden has been authorized and is now taking orders for free hay, and some of it has been already ordered and is on the way to Antigonish. The following telegram has been received by Mr. Whidden from one of the largest hay dealers in the Maritime provinces:
Amherst, N.S., January 13, 1913.
C. Edgar Whidden,
Consignment of hay to you going forward at once. Any other orders will be promptly attended to. You get hay free of freight charges for farmers only.
(Sgd.) Edgar Fillmore.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Was that dispatch not correct?

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say it was correct?

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Well, I will quote the Minister to prove that it was not correct, that it was absolutely untrue. My hon. friend should not jump before he reaches the stile. What I have read was what was sent out on January 14, and the election was on the 16th. The electors were told they were going to 'get free hay.' Now, let me deal with the question asked by my hon. friend. On page 3271 of 'Hansard' of February 13, 1913, he will find that I asked the following question:
1.	Referring to a telegram purporting to have been received by one C. Edgar Whidden from one of the hay dealers in Amherst, Cumberland county, during the recent by-election for the provincial legislature in Antigonish county, as follows:-
Amherst, N.S., January 13, 1913.
C. Edgar Whidden,
Antigonish.
Consignment of hay to you going forward at once, any other orders will be promptly attended to. You get hay free of freight charges for farmers only.
(Sgd.) Edgar Fillmore.
2.	Was any arrangement made by the Department of Railways, or any of its officials, for free carriage of hay over the Intercolonial railway from Amherst to Antigonish, as stated in said telegram?
3.	Has there been free or reduced transportation for carrying hay over any part of the

Intercolonial, or any reduction or rebate made to shippers or purchasers of hay for Antigonish county since the beginning of the present year?
Mr. Cochrane answered 'no' to each of those questions; there was no free transportation, no reduction, no rebate. One would suppose that with that record before them, the Conservative party would be thoroughly abashed in Antigonish county, and they would cease from referring to this matter any further. But, like my hon. friends opposite who have been interrupting me, they did not seem to grasp the humiliation in which the minister and the government were placed by their desperate efforts to win the constituency. _ After the elections were over, Senator Girroir wrote in the Casket of February 6, 1913, as follows:
Notwithstanding any rumours or assertions to the contrary, arrangements have been made for the importation of hay into this county from Amherst and vicinity, and the delivery of same to Antigonish farmers at the price for which it is purchased there. The farmer gets his hay for the price at which it is sold in the open market at Amherst or vicinity, and neither directly nor indirectly pays any freight or other charges on same from that district. We have asked the following leading citizens to make a thorough investigation into the whole matter, and publish a report of their findings in the Casket, and they have consented to do so:
A. D. Chisholm, merchant.
George Taylor, Esq., farmer.
Dan D. McDonald, merchant.
James H. Stewart, merchant.
H. H. Crearar, Esq., farmer.
I will give any person who will furnish satisfactory evidence to disprove the above statement the sum of two hundred dollars.
I do not know to what statement he refers, whether it is to the statement that hay can be bought at Amherst at market prices, or that those people had been appointed a committee. Then he proceeded:
Farmers should order their hay at once as this privilege cannot he held open later than March 15th inst. Advices are to the effect that at present there is a heavy demand from Newfoundland and other places, which is liable to cause an advance in price in the very near future.	.
E. Lavin Giro)*-.
Antigonish, N.S., February 5, 1913.
So far as the gentlemen who constituted the committee are concerned, I may point out that they were not appointed by the Farmers' Association. We have no knowledge of who appointed them. I may also point out that they are all Conservatives with one exception, and the exception is a gentleman whose name I was surprised to find in the list, for he has always home a reputation for integrity, fail dealing, and honour in all his business relations. I am surprised to find that he had any finger in such a scheme as this, and that he should Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish!
so far forget himself as to lend his name to such a deception of the public. There was an alleged investigation, and the report of those Conservatives who constituted uie body of white-washers was that they could not find where freight had been charged. Let me call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that on March 3 I moved:
For a statement of all amounts collected by the Intercolonial railway for freight on hay carried from Amherst and other stations on the Intercolonial, county of Cumberland, to Antigonish, N.S., and consigned to C. Edgar Whidden or C. B. Whidden & Son, in the month of January last and Februarv instant, and by whom such freight was paid; also a copy of all way bills and bills of lading for the same.-Mr. Chisholm (Antigonish).
The papers were brought down and among them a letter from Mr. Pottinger, as follows:
In reply I beg to advise that we have no record of any carloads of hay carried from Amherst and other stations on the Intercolonial railway in the county of Cumberland to Amherst, N.S., and consigned to Edgar Whidden or C. B. Whidden & iSon in the months of January ajjd February.
According to the return that was brought down on March 27, there was no hay sent to C. B. Whidden or C. Edgar Whidden; yet, the telegram of Edward Fillmore to C. Edgar Whidden. is that he is sending hay and there are no freight charges upon it. Yet, this whitewashing committee, that looked into the books of the Messrs. Whidden, cannot find where a single cent has been charged the farmers for hay. Let us dispose of this thing once and for all. The statement of the Prime Minister is on 'Hansard'to the effect that there was no free transportation, the statement of the Minister of Railways and Canals is there that there was no free transportation of hay over any portion of the Intercolonial railway since the 1st January, 1912, and that there was no rebate or remission of any kind so far as freight rates are concerned. The fact is that the farmers were purchasing their hay from Amherst and other sections, they were paying freight upon it and they were able to get it at as cheap a figure, within fifty cents a ton, as the price at which it wa3 sold through the Conservative party. And the hay got through the Conservative Committee was very inferior. This whole free hay arrangement was a scheme to deceive and mislead the people. It is the old st-ory that, following corruption you will find deception, dishonesty and untruthfulness. When the Minister of Public Works started the thing in the beginning of the campaign by publishing these fake estimates and by seeking to bribe the electors in platoons it was followed by his friends with deception.

dishonesty and untruthfulness and since that time they have floundered until now there is none so poor as to do them reverence in Antigonish county. I would like to direct the attention of the House to the way in which the Minister of Railways and Canals is building railways for Antigonish county.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: PROPOSED CENSURE OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Before six o'clock I
was referring to the way in which the Conservative party sought to use the question of free transportation of hay over the Intercolonial in order to influence the election that took place. I pointed out that according to the statement of the Minister of Railways in this House there was no free transportation of hay over the Intercolonial railway. Let me refer to the answer made by the Minister of Railways on the 20th of January, 1913, ('Hansard' page 1786) to a question put by my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte). Remember this was a few days after the by-election took place in Antigonish:
Mr. Kyte: I desire to ask a question of the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals. I beg to read the following telegram, which I received on Saturday:
Arichat, N.S., 17th Jan., 1913. f 6. W. Kyte, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Council directs me to wire to know if free transportation hay Intercolonial railway has been granted.
D. H. Campbell,
Municipal Clerk.
It is desired to know if any arrangement has been made for free transportation of hay on the Intercolonial railway.
Mr. Cochrane:	I have taken the attitude
all along that if anything is done in that respect, it should be done by a special vote, and not by the Intercolonial.
The reason I labour this is to meet the remark made by the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) which would convey the impression that free transportation had been granted on the Intercolonial. To set the matter at rest so far as the farmers of Antigonish county are concerned,
I state that they had to pay for the hay they imported. Let me quote the statement made by the Prime Minister on the 10th of February, 1913-'Hansard' page 3123:
Mi'. Borden:	Before moving the adjournment of the House I wish to give some information to my hon. friend from Antigonish who made inquiry a few days ago with regard to representations to the Government from certain eastern counties of Nova Scotia as to providing free transportation of hay on the Intercolonial railway. The Government have had under consideration representations received from the counties of Antigonish and Guysborough and from the Island of Cape

Breton, with regard to the shortage of hay in that district and the advisability of granting free transportation over the Intercolonial railway. It seemed better that any necessary aid should be given not by free transportation but by a money grant so that there would be no discrimination in such cases between portions of Canada served by the Intercolonial railway and those served by other railways. The Government being desirous of doing anything that could reasonably be undertaken for the purpose of aiding the farmers of the district above mentioned made very careful inquiry through the Department of Agriculture and otherwise into the conditions in eastern Nova Scotia and Cape Breton. The result of that inquiry has not established conditions which would justify a special grant. In some counties there was undoubtedly a regrettable shortage in the hay crop, but unless a definite policy of special aid in all cases of crop shortage is to be entered upon there seems no justification for acceding to the requests that have been made for Government assistance in this instance. According to the reports made to the Government the conditions are not nearly so severe and the shortage is not nearly so great as in 1904 and the reports made to the Government indicate that there is a considerable surplus above requirements in the -western part of the provinces ind in New Brunswick.
There is no question in the mind of the Prime Minister as to what the farmers of the eastern section of Nova Scotia and the farmers of Antigonish wanted, namely, free transportation of hay on the Intercolonial. Let me direct attention to the fact that in 1904 when there was a scarcity of hay in eastern Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, hay was carried free of freight charge from the province of Quebec. I also direct attention to the fact that the Prime Minister in making this statement on the 10th of February, 1913, knew that the Minister of Railways had as early as October 12, and even earlier, stated that there should be no free transportation. Let me further call attention to the fact that the Prime Minister kept back this information until the election was over. I stated before six o'clock that on the 15th December in answer to a question of mine as to whether there was, or would be, free transportation or not on the Intercolonial, the minister stated that the matter was under consideration. I should have stated it was on the 12th December, and not on the 15th of December, that the answer was given. The Prime Minister knew, and every member of his Government knew, that they had no intention of allowing free transportation of hay, and what I complain of is the deception that was practiced on the people of eastern Nova Scotia. That is not the worst feature of it. The worst feature of it is found in the fact that certain ministers, not only one but several, should be guilty of such deception and dishonesty. What will the people of

the country think of our public men; what confidence can they have in our public men when ministers of the Crown will descend to such small tactics for the purpose of furthering their ends. My hon. friend from Annapolis intimated that the people of Antigonish received their hay free of transportation charges. I read a letter from Senator Girroir in which he offers to bet a sum of money that his statements were correct in that regard. He refers also to a certain committee that was appointed, but as to who had the appointment of that committee we are in the dark. Certainly the Farmers' Association did not appoint that committee, and so far as I can see there are no Liberals on it. In order that you may see the desperation of these men, let me quote the report of that committee, composed of the henchmen of Senator Girroir:
Report on Free Transportation of Hay.
We, the undersigned, duly app inted to ascertain whether the hay for farmers, which has been and is now being imported into this county from Amherst and vicinity by C. Edgar Whidden has been and is being imported free of freight charges to farmers of Antigonish county, beg to report as follows:
1. That we have examined all books, vouchers, letters, telegrams, invoices, bills of lading and quotations in the hands of the said C. Edgar Whidden relating to the importation of the said hay, and have ourselves obtained quotations from dealers, and find that all hay so far imported by Mr. Whidden has been sold to farmers at the selling price of said hay in the open market at Amherst and vicinty; and that no freight charges from Amherst and vicinity have either directly or indirectly been charged the farmers on said hay. We further state, that this hay is being bought at the lowest market price at Amherst and vicinity, and is sold to farmers at this price. Farmers not only receive this hay free of freight charges, but pay no commission or charges of any kind for the ordering, handling or distributing of said hay.
We further undertake to see that all hay so imported up to the 15th of March next shall be sold to farmers under the same conditions as above set forth.
Dated at Antigonish, N.S., the 17th day of February, 1913.
J. G. Taylor,
A. D. Chisholm,
D. D. MacDonald,
J. H. Stewart,
H. H. Crerar.
I do not know whether the gentlemen whose names are appended to this report signed it or not, but I do know that after the other notice regarding free transportation arrangements was published in the Casket, the week before the election, with the name of P. S. Floyd, a respectable and prominent citizen of Antigonish, a Liberal, he repudiated it as soon as he had an opportunity of doing so, and stated that he Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
had not authorized his name to be put to the document. I do not know whether the signatures of these gentlemen, purporting to be genuine, are genuine or not, but in view of the falsification of documents and the liberties taken with the names of citizens of the town and county in connection with this matter, I would not be surprised if some day or other these men would repudiate this report. According to the information that was brought down to this House a few days ago by the Minister of Railways, there was no hay shipped to C. Edgar Whidden. According to the committee's report, there was, but no freight was paid. It is certain, however, that the farmers of the county of Antigonish paid the freight on hay. The Minister of Railways more than once said that there was no free transportation, rebate, or remission of any kind so far as freight was concerned. The farmers have had to pay the freight cn this hay and the attempt of Senator Girroir, his henchmen and the committee which had been appointed by him, to bolster up this weak case of theirs is absolutely futile. There is no question of the fret that the hay that was imported by these people was hay of an inferior quality; in fact it was so bad that a good deal of it was sent back. I would infer from a remark made by the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) that he contends that the farmers of Antigonish county did not pay this freight. I desire to say that the freight was paid by them indirectly. It is true that they did not put their hands in their pockets when they were purchasing the hay and pay the freight upon it. Likely the freight was prepaid; or if not, the hay sent was of a very inferior quality, and the farmers were paying for a third quality when they thought they were getting a better quality. Those who purchased hay outside of the nominee of Senator Girroir and the Tory party, paid freight on it and got it at practically the same price, better hay, than was received through the nominee of the Tories on that occasion.
I wish to refer to another canvass that was made on that occasion, and that is with respect to railway facilities. I had occasion to ask the Minister of Railways during the- session whether he had received any report with regard to the proposed line of railway between Antigonish and Country Harbour, and he replied that he had not. The minister promised me a year ago last February that a survey of that line would be made, but that promise, I regret to say, has not been fulfilled. During the election campaign a man who pretended to have authority for making the statement, appealed to the people to support the Conservative candidate because they had the

assurance that this line of railway would be constructed. Among the numerous campaign documents that were issued was one from which the following is an extract [DOT]
About a year ago, Hon. F. Cochrane, Minister of Railways, on his first visit to Nova Scotia, invited representations and information with respect to proposed railways in the province. Shortly afterwards, I placed myself in communication with the department, and * have had considerable correspondence with him during the past ten months, on the question of branch line from Cape George to Country Harbour, instead of the Sunnybrae route through Pictou county.
I moved for all the correspondence in connection with that matter, and although I have made inquiries from the Department of Railways I can find no correspondence of this nature on the public files. The writer of this document goes on to say that two eminent engineers made a cursory examination of the road. If a report was made by those engineers, I would ask the Minister of Railways, if he were here, why that report is not available. He goes on to say further:
Some there are, who say this promised survey is just now only for election purposes. I can safely assure them, knowing what I do, that it is not, and knowing Hon. Mr. Cochrane as I now do, from lengthy correspondence, I am fully convinced that he is one of the last public men in Canada, who would stoop to any sinister purposes. He is not a man of promises, but if he makes any, he fulfills it.
I would like to know why this lengthy correspondence is not on file.
As early as February 22 last, in a letter to me, which I now hold, he wrote:
I can assure you that the railway interests of the district you refer to, will not be lost sight of.
In a letter dated April 11th last, he wrote:-
I hope to be able to look into the railway situation in Nova Scotia some time during the month of May.
Where is that correspondence? If this man has been corresponding with the minister and has put him in possession of such information as he has alleged, why does that correspondence not appear on the public file, and why do not hon. gentlemen of this House have access to it? I rather think that if such correspondence ever existed it was consigned to the waste-basket, where the minister probably thought it deserved to be plaoed. There are some references to this document which would seem to indicate that the writer was the first person to call the attention of the Government to the necessity for this railway. Let me, however, call your attention to the fact that on more that one occasion -in fact during every session of Parliament since I first had the honour of occupying a seat in this House-I called the
323i
attention of the Government to the necessity for the construction of this road, and I had a promise from the minister that a survey would be made long before the gentleman who wrote this document had made his alleged appeals to the minister.
The object of my amendment is to call the attention of the House and the country to some of t/he political methods, some of the extraordinary actions of the Minister of Public works, which, unless checked, are fraught with great danger to the country. Taking it all in all, there is a sense of political decency, honour and honesty throughout Canada. Here and there occasionally, acts are done, political warfare carried on in an improper and reprehensible manner. But the heart of the people as a whole to-day is sound. It was not always thus. It is not many years since Canadians had to blush for the corruption in this country and the misdeeds in high places. So disgraceful had these things become that the English press, irrespective of party, referred to them as Canada's shame, and a certain respected and honoured clergyman in Canada, one of the leading Canadians of his time, exclaimed in the bitterness of his soul, ' as well defend Sodom as to try to defend these acts of political corruption.' I desire to refer to some of the comments of the English press in this connection. The London Times, speaking of the corruption of these days:
What is the date?

This was previous to 1896, before the cleaning up the country got after the Liberal party came into power. I mention this to show hon. gentlemen that we seem to be reverting back to a similar condition of affairs, and, unless there is a change from the conditions connected with the Macdonald, Richelieu and Antigonish elections, we will be back again to the shameful and disgraceful conditions that existed when the English press commented in such denunciatory terms of the state of public and political life in Canada. The London Times said:
Here in the Mother Country there can be
only one feeling, that of deep regret for the wrong done to the fair fame of the eldest of her daughters.	\
The London Graphic said:
It is no longer possible to doubt that corruption in its worst form is rampant in a large portion of the Canadian civil service.
This is from the London Telegraph:
Enough unfortunately is already known in1 England to make it clear that only the most resolute and drastic purification can redeem' public life in Canada from the taint of corruption, the like of which we have not seen in our own country for hundreds of years.
The Graphic Despatch had this to say:

Even Tammany Hall smells sweet and clean in comparison witli the huge stink pot of the Conservative Government.
In Sir Richard Cartwright's memoirs there is a black chapter on Canadian shame, where this matter is fully discussed and commented upon. Making due allowance for the intensity of that distinguished statesman's feelings and his extremely keen sense of honour, every fair-minded man, Conservative as well as Liberal, has to admit with sorrow and regret that what Sir Richard Cartwright wrote was, alas, too true. He was in a position to know; he was a contemporary of the events narrated. His memoirs were not to be published until after death; he had no interest in exaggerating, or minimizing the facts; his statements were in the nature of dying declarations, and they have not been controverted in any material respect. It is with shame and regret, I say, we recognize the truth of the facts of Canadian history, as pictured by him. But there is a brighter side. The exposure of the iniquities perpetrated in the days of Sir John A. Macdonald aroused the public conscience and since then a better and healthier state of public sentiment has been created. Sir Mackenzie Bowell was an honest man; Sir John Thomson had a high sense of public duty and was a man of honour, and honesty. Sir Wilfrid Laurier gave the country an honest administration, and the present Prime Minister of Canada was expected to govern the country honestly. The present Prime Minister had a reputation for honesty and integrity in private life and he was regarded, when he took the reins of office, as a man of high political ideas, with a due sense of political rectitude, who could be depended on to give effect to these, ideas in the administration of public affairs. Unfortunately at the very outset of his career he proved somewhat of a disappointment to the best element of his party and the country generally, when he formed the unholy alliance with the extreme wing, the supposedly disloyal element in our country-the Nationalists of Quebec. In the formation of his Government the people were surprised to find him surrounding himself with the Nationalists from Quebec and another extreme element from the province of Ontario, whose counterpart in the old country, in Ulster, Ireland, openly threatened the Crown but a few months ago. But it is not these conflicting elements, this heterogeneous combination of which I desre to speak. Great as was the surprise of the country at the unholy alliance, there was greater surprise when the present Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Railways were called by the Prime Minister to be among the advisers of the Governor General. What
Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish!
qualifications did these men possess that they should be selected over the heads of better men in the ranks of the Conservative party? Everybody will admit that these men in point of ability and intellectual force and attainments were much inferior to members who sit on the other side of the House, whom I might mention. But the stalwarts who fought the battles of their party when they were in Opposition, were passed over, and these outsiders were given the preference. Why was this, people wondered. The explanation of it all is that the Minister of Public Works is skilled in election methods, he has said so himself, he declared that he was a master at winning elections. There is such a thing as Skill in the management of elections that will be the undoing of the party in whose favour such methods are employed, and I venture to predict that the day is not far distant when the Prime Minister will find that such methods as have been adopted by the Minister of Public Works in Macdonald, Richelieu and Antigonish will bring a sad and sorry day for the Conservative party and will be the wreck and ruin of that party in the not distant future.
I regret that I have had to take up so much of the time of the House but I think I have shown you conclusively that the Minister of Public Works, in sending that letter, was guilty of a breach of the privileges of this House. I say that no minister should be permitted to divulge the estimates in advance, to make public a document of a secret character such as this before it is submitted to Parliament. I submit that in doing so he violated the rights and privileges of this House. His conduct in writing that letter, by his secretary, and stating that there were certain estimates for Antigonish county when, as a matter of fact, the main estimates had not been prepared and the supplementary had not been under consideration, was, besides being untrue, a breach of faith 'towards his colleagues and a violation of his o'ath as a privy councillor. I have read that oath, I have quoted to you what the authorities say on the duties of a privy councillor. There is no doubt that a cabinet minister is not permitted to disclose what has taken place in council. In giving any information about what was contained in the estimates, or would be, he was guilty of a breach of faith towards his colleagues and violating his duty as a privy councillor. His conduct in offering to the electors of Antigonish public works if they delivered the goods is conduct that will pieet with the disapproval of every man in this House and out of it. At the very inception of this whole matter there was an unlawful bargain made between the

Prime Minister of Canada and the appointee to the Senate whose elevation caused the vacancy in the legislature that brought on the election. It is no secret that Senator Girroir could not have got his appointment as a Senator had there not been given to the Prime Minister an assurance that the county of Antigonish would return a supporter of the Opposition in the local Legislature. I say that a contract of that kind is corrupt and dishonest and should meet with the disapproval of every right thinking man in this House and outside of it.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman is
entitled to nothing else, he is at least entitled to congratulation upon his own patience with himself. For months this House has been threatened with the attack which has just been made by the hon. member for Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm). We have listened, as we were bound to listen, for upwards of two hours to-day to my hon. friend, and as far as I can judge the only thing that he has been able to accomplish is to reflect upon the honour, the honesty and the intelligence of the electors of the county who have done him the honour of sending him to this Parliament to represent them. He accuses me of having caused a letter to be written which he claims to have had the effect of purchasing, almost holus bolus, his honest electors in Antigonish in a by-election a few months ago.

I said no such thing.
I said there was an attempt but I distinctly stated that the people of Antigonish could not be bought.

I can assure my hon.
friend in the first place that he is very much mistaken. I have a great deal too much confidence in the honour and in the honesty and in the intelligence of the citizens of that constituency to venture to believe or to think that either a letter from myself or any action upon my part or upon the part of any other individual in this Dominion of Canada would have the effect of purchasing any individual within the borders of that intelligent constituency of Antigonish. In the second place, let me say to my hon. friend that the letter, which he accuses me of having had distributed in this constituency was, I understand, written upon the 28th day of December, when I was in the city of Winnipeg, endeavouring to enjoy my Christmas holidays. I had no knowledge of any kind or description that any such letter had been written, and no knowledge so far as requests from Senator Girroir or any other person were concerned, that a by-election was taking place in the county represented by my hon. friend.
Now let me explain and make clear to the House what did happen. For some time
previous, Senator Girroir had been taking an interest in the welfare of the constituency in which he lived. He had appealed to the officers of the Department of Public Works, he had appealed to my predecessor in office and had pointed out to him the necessity that, in his opinion, existed for the expenditure of a certain amount of public money in the public interest in that particular locality. He had succeeded in persuading my predecessor in office and the officers of the department that his requests were, at all events, entitled to serious consideration, and to this extent, Mr. Speaker, he succeeded in having placed in that department certain items to be noted for consideration when the estimates came up. In view of the several requests which he had made in this form, it appears that he addressed to myself a letter, which arrived at the department at a time when I was in the city of Winnipeg, and it was answered by my secretary. In the light of the knowledge which my secretary had of the circumstances, of the fact that Senator Girroir had been interesting himself in securing, if he possibly could, necessary public works in that particular locality and that Senator Girroir had full knowledge of the manner in which those estimates were considered and provided for from time to time-in view of these circumstances Mr. Speaker, I claim that my secretary was quite justified in writing the letter which he addressed to Senator Girroir. But he was careful to attach to that letter a statement of the amount that Senator Girroir had asked to be placed in the estimates for the carrying on of necessary public works in the constituency, for he headed his statement in the following words:
List of Amounts ifor Antigonish county, Nova Scotia, noted for the estimates of 1913-14.
That is apparently all that my hon. friend has to complain of. It is true, Sir, that he undertakes to complain that a certain mutilation of this statement took place in a certain newspaper in the constituency which he represents. But, Mr. Speaker, I am at a loss to know now whether or not my hon. friend from Antigonish accuses the editor of that newspaper in his constituency of being the individual guilty of the mutilation of that statement. In that respect he has not made himself clear to this House, and I am sure he will not make his statement clear to the editor of that newspaper. I do not know whether I am to understand from his remarks this afternoon that he objects to the items which Senator Girroir was successful in having noted for consideration in the supplementary estimates that are to be brought down to this House at a later date.

I said distinctly that
I approved of them.

I did not understand my hon. friend to make it clear whether or not he desires this expenditure of public money in the constituency which he represents. Let me say to my hon. friend that it was only on Saturday last that, as Minister of Public Works, I had the time and opportunity to give any consideration to the items which were noted for the supplementary estimates in respect to the constituency of Antigonish, and if may hon. friend would take the responsibility, in line with his arguments to-day, of saying that he does not want this money spent in that locality, he might influence me in my recommendation to this House with respect to what Senator Girroir suggested should be expended in the public interest in this particular locality.

I stated distinctly
that you owed it to yourself, to the Government, and to the reputation of Senator Girroir that you should have those items in the supplementary ' estimates. They would form an antidote to the poison which was contained in the cup. of humilitation that the Tories of Antigonish had to drink when that letter was published.

I am glad to get a definite statement, at all events, from my hon. friend in respect to his desire that some money, at least, should be spent in his particular constituency. I do not know, however, that his arguments and his misrepresentation of the actual facts will assist him in getting for his constituency the full benefit that the public necessities of that portion of the Dominion deserve. I want to say to my hon. friend in a word, because I do not propose to occupy more than a minute or two of the time of this House in replying to the rambling statement which he undertook to make this afternoon, that when the next election takes place in that constituency in my opinion it will not be necessary for the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Railways, or myself, to write any letter, or to give any consideration to the freight upon hay, or to anything else in that locali-ity, for all that will be necessary will be for the Conservative candidate, whoever he may be, to -take the speech delivered by my hon. friend this afternoon and place it in the hands of every intelligent elector in that constituency. They will find in that speech a reflection upon their honour and upon their honesty by the man whom they sent to this Parliament as their trusted representative. And I believe that speech will be sufficient to assure the election of a Conservative candidate, who will follow in the footsteps of Senator Girroir and come down to this Parliament seized of his responsibilities, seized of his duties to the constituency, and will present as best he can their claims for the carrying on of certain public works Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
in that constituency in a manner that will be creditable to the Government and satisfactory to the electors. My hon. friend who has gone very wide of the amendment which he has proposed and has undertaken to deal with certain conditions with respect to the freight upon hay as dealt with by the Minister of Railways and Canals. He goes to the length of accusing the Prime Minister of being guilty of dishonesty in this matter in order that it might affect the result of a byj-election in Nova Scotia. I think, Sir, that the argument of the hon. gentleman is so ridiculous, if argument he did make, that it needs no answer from me. I am free to confess that after having listened to him as attentively as I could, I do not know now whether he was complaining that the farmers of Antigonish county were successful in getting hay at free rates over the Intercolonial railway. The remarks of my hon. friend were so mixed and disconnected that I am at a loss to know now what was his complaint in this regard as against the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways. I am convinced that neither the Prime Minister nor the Minister of Railways made any statement in connection with the matter that was pot in keeping with the dignity of their position, with the dignity and the rules of this Parliament, and in accordance with their duty as representatives of the people of Canada. I am surprised that my hon. friend should have occupied the time of the House in presenting here "the very simple matter which he has presented and which has already been answered in this Parliament, I am sure to the satisfaction of every hon. member. The facts are as I have stated: That the letter which my hon. friend complains of was simply written to Senator Girroir, who had undertaken to have placed in the estimates, if he possibly could, certain items which he desired to have considered in connection with the expenditure of certain public money in the public interest in that particular constituency. And in doing so, Senator Girroir, in my opinion, was fulfilling a service to that constituency and to that locality, and deserved well of the people there. And we have here to-day the spectacle of the man who was elected as the representative of that constituency coming forward in his own simple form and endeavouring to reflect upon the honour and upon the honesty of those who entrusted him with their confidence and sent him to this Parliament to look after their best interests and to see that their constituency should receive its full share of public money in order that it might have the same measure of prosperity in the development of its industrial life that should come to every constituency within the

borders of this Dominion of Canada. I will only add that I am satisfied that when the speech of my hon. friend is read by his constituents it will meet the same fate as the amendment in this Parliament, that of being turned down by every intelligent hearer who gives consideration to the simple and very disconnected manner in which he has ventured to occupy the time of this House for over two hours.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton and Victoria):
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Antigonish (Mr. Chisnolm) in my opinion has made out a very strong case against the Minister of Public Works, and, so far as I can understand the answer of the minister, it is an absolutely undefended case. I see opposite me quite a number of able advocates, men who are accustomed to defending cases in the courts, particularly in the criminal courts- as this is to some extent a quasi-criminal charge, and I submit to them that I do speak it truly when I say that if this case were before a judge and jury in view of the evidence that was put forward by the hon. member for Antigonish and of the answer or statement of the minister himself, the judge would have to tell the jury that the case was not defended at all and that there was nothing left for them to do but to give a verdict of guilty upon the facts as represented to them. The form and substance of the statement of the Minister of Public Works is that in any county in Canada in which there is an election pending it is perfectly open to any minister of the Crown, months. and months before the estimates are prepared and long before they are sanctioned by the Governor General, to make copies of them and send them broadcast throughout the constituency to tell the electors that this is what the county is going to get, this is what we are going to do for you, and this is what we are going to do for you particularly if you vote for our candidate. That is the case presented as a defence by a gentleman of the experience and standing in this country of this minister of the Crown. I submit to any minister of the Crown here that this offer of money to be expended in the constituency in a particular way so that it will go into the pockets of the people, is as much bribery in the eyes of the law, just as corrupt as if the_ minister had gone from house to house giving the money into ..the people's hands. I ask the Minister of Public Works as a man of experience in the affairs of the world, particularly of experience as he boasts himself in the winning of elections, what was this letter published for? That is what we ask. What did Senator Girroir ask the letter for? And I ask, why was not Senator Girroir's letter produced? If this is an open-minded honest statement made to the public, why are we
not given a knowledge of the communication that Senator Girroir sent to the minister? That would be illuminating, I am sure, and we would know whether things really are as they are attempted to be made appear in this connection. That letter is suppressed. There may be nothing in it, but so far it has not been given to the public. The minister says that this letter was published in good faith. We are not in ignorance of wliat took place around this House and around the office of the minister before Parliament rose at Christmas, when he went off on his joyous trip to Winnipeg. He knows that the Opposition in the local legislature of Nova Scotia was here, he knows that every local member supporting the Opposition was here, he knows that they called upon him one by one, or together, and put to him the great necessity of carrying this by-election in Antigonish at all costs.

The hon. gentleman is
entirely in error. I do not recollect any non. gentleman mentioning the by-election that took place.
They saw Buskard.

They saw this Gilpin
Homer, who was in his office, and, if my hon. friend read Scott's Lay of the Last Minstrel, he will find out who this Gilpin Horner was. He was a man who could be blamed for everything. If they did not see the minister
That is a romance.

If I am romancing, I have only to go for happy fellowship across the way. That is the condition of things. Before the election the whole outfit of the Opposition came up here, got the sinews of war in shape and the way it was arranged with the minister was that Senator Girroir was to go home to Nova Scotia and there write a letter.

I absolutely deny that
statement.

Gilpin Homer again;
blame him for it. If you charge the hon. Minister of Public Works with a'violation of any of the Ten Commandments, he will get up and say: I absolutely deny it from start to finish. But there is such a thing as exhausting these denials. They are getting very stale now.
They are not as stale as your charges.

This is a synchronism, ft is a well known fact to many hon. mem->ers of this House that no action can be. and never was, taken on the estimates until they have finally passed and the House pro-

rogues. Instructions then go to the officers of the Government in different parts of tne country to put into execution the votes that are passed. That is the course which tiie minister should have taken when he received that letter, or that it is the course that should have been taken by his secretary. If his secretary wanted to act in a straight, honest and above-board fashion, he would have written a letter acknowledging the receipt of the letter which had come to him and he should have told Senator Girroir that the minister was out of the city, that he was away on his Christmas holidays, that he would be back in due time and that he would lay the senator's letter before him. That is what an honest business-like above-board officer would have done with Senator Girroir's letter. But it was found that this would not do, that there was haste necessary, that the business would not wait, that there was a by-eleotion to be run in Antigonish and that to give the information when the minister came back would not answer the purpose of their friends in that county. Therefore, this letter went out, a letter which had no business to go out.
Will the Minister dare to say that there is any justification for any minister under the Crown to give any information of this character? The only message that comes into this House, when we are all standing up solemnly, and with bared heads, is the message which we receive from the representative of the King transmitting the Estimates. It is on such an occasion as this that this act of solemnity is performed. But we have a minister of the Crown who cares nothing about these solemnities, who cares nothing about the dignity which hitherto has surrounded occasions of this kind but who will write a letter and place in that letter the estimates which are to he and send them broadcast for the purpose of corrupting the people of this country. An attempt has been made to throw back, in reference to my hon. friend from Antigonish, that he is casting a reflection upon his people because, forsooth, this effort has been made. Is that any reflection upon the good people of Antigonish? On the contrary, the Minister of Public Works did not understand the kind of people they were. Is it any credit to him that the bait was not swallowed in the county of Antigonish? He did everything he could and he now tries to frighten the hon. member for Antigonish by saying that:	When the next election comes on
we will publish your speech and -tell the people that you thought they could be bought. My hon. friend from Antigonish said nothing'of the kind. He is not the man who thought they could be bought, but the men who thought they could be bought were the minister and his Senator who went and placed this bait before them.
Mr. McKEINZIE
If, I repeat, there is one thing more than another that should be respected in this country, it is the judgment that people are to give through the medium of the ballot box. Men should go to the ballot box unprejudiced and willing to pass judgment upon the record of the party that is on trial. 1 submit that no action of this Government was on trial in the Antigonish election, that the Minister of Public Works had no business to interfere in that election, neither was the Government on trial, but the conduct of another -government altogether apart from this Government was placed before the people, and they were called upon to pass judgment upon it. The electors of Antigonish were the jurors who were to pass judgment upon the conduct of the Government of the province of Nova Scotia and what think you, Sir, of this Government, and what think you of a Minister of Public Works who would be willing to stuff the pockets of the jury with his money in order that they might -bring in a false verdict? That is the position in which he stands and that is the position in which those behind him stand who sneer and laugh at the idea that there was anything wrong in going to the people of Antigonish with something like $200,000 of money and saying to them: vote for O'Brien and you will get this money, but if you do not vote for O'Brien, if you dare to open your mouths against this conduct of promising this money, I will see to it that you will not get it. That is giving us a fair sample of what we were talking about in this House for some weeks -the use to which the Road Act is to be put by the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), and the use that the agricultural subsidy Act is to be put by the hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell). When a man in any province expresses an honest, fearless opinion he will be told: You are not going to allow this money to be spent in your province, you do not want the money, and therefore you must shut your mouth and say nothing.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to
a point of order. My hon. friend is using language that he is absolutely unjustified in using. He has stated that the use that I will make of the money voted for the promotion of agriculture will be that I will withhold it unless -certain things are done in a constituency. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is an offensive expression.

I did not say anything of the kind. T said we had a fair sample, in a speech of the hon. the Minister of Public Works to-night, of what would happen if a man from any county or province would dare to express an independent opinion about the expenditure in his county or province. He would be threatened that he

would be demolished by the people of that county or province if he dared to do so.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member is
giving a very plain illustration, but I am not sure that the point of order is well taken; I think the language used by the hon. member can properly be used.

I rather think it is
more or less beneath the dignity of a member of the Canadian House of Lords, that he should go around looking after affairs of this kind or trying to corrupt the electors in any part of the Dominion. We are told that the functions of a senator should be higher than that of a party hack; we are led to believe a senator is on a high plane where he is to hold evenly the balance between different opinions in this House and carry out what may be regarded as best for the country generally. But I find that Senator Girror does not regard himself in that light. I have nere a manifesto, a manifesto mind you, issued by that gentleman on the 20th December, 1912, asking the support of the people of Antigonish for his candidate in this provincial election. Among other things he says:
A vote for John S. O'Brien will be an expression of confidence in the Government of the day at Ottawa.
By what circumlocution can a vote one way or the other upon the conduct of the Murray Government in Nova Scotia be a vote of confidence or non-confidence in the Ottawa Government ? He says further:
A vote for Mr. O'Brien will strengthen my hand in my endeavor on your behalf.
