Well, the meaning of that is: If you vote for Mr. O'Brien, you will get $3,000 for Arisaig; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien, you will get $2,500 for Bayfield; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien, you will get $8,200 for Blue Rock; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien, you will get $1,400 for Breen's Pond; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien, you will get $1,000 for Harbour au Boucher; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien you will get $800 for Malignant Cove; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien you will get $15,000 for Crib-bons Point; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien you will get $14,700 for Delorey's Beach; if you vote for	Mr.	O'Brien	you will get	another $4,000	for	Malignant Cove; if	youvote for Mr. O'Brien you will get $1,700 for McArra's Brook; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien you will get $5,500 for McNair's Cove; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien you will get $2,800 for Ogdens Pond; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien	you	will get	$3,000 for SouthLakevale; if	you	vote for	Mr. O'Brien	you
will get $15,000 for Auld's Cove; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien you will get $27,000 for Tracadie Harbour; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien you will get $1,200 for Harbour-au Boucher; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien you
will get another $14,500 for Breen's Pond; if you vote for Mr. O'Brien you will get $90,000 for a new wharf at Georgeville. And then, to wind up, if you vote for Mr. O'Brien there will also be placed in the general vote for dredging, amounts for Lakevale and Bayfield and an amount to repair the old wharf at Georgeville. Georgeville is a country place where there is not much shipping and true there is an old wharf there, but if you vote for O'Brien we will repair the old wharf and build a new wharf at a cost $90,000 so that you may be able to distinguish the difference between the two. The practice generally is to vote a lump sum for each province for dredging, but in this case the minister through his agent told the people of Antigonish that the usual practice was to be departed from and that there was to be a special vote for dredging in that county. You will see, therefore, what was meant by Senator Girroir' when he wrote this letter on the 27th of December, which was sent to every elector in the county. I would haVe no fault to find if these estimates eame out in the-proper way, but I characterize it as robbery of the darkest and most high-handed character in a political sense to publish these estimates at that time. The minister tells us now that he had not considered them; they certainly were not before council at the time, and possibly some of them have not gone before Council yet. I understand that matters of this kind first go before the department, whence they are sent to the Minister of Finance, who puts them down, and finally they get to council where they are carved further and until they are laid on the table of the House nobody can tell what money it is intended to expend. That is the proper way; that is the way it ought to be; that is the way it used to be both under Conservatives and Liberals until a new chapter has been introduced into the political history of this country by a minister who wants to win elections no matter what it may cost. It is the Minister of Elections and not the Minister of Public Works who has charge of this now, and as minister of winning elections he is not to be circumscribed. Trivialities are not to interfere with him in the slightest, and this false information could go to the country to enable him to win an election whether it is right or wrong. I submit, Mr. Speaker, there is no justification for conduct of this kind, and I put the question again: what was the purpose of this announcement in the midst of an election; why was there not decency enough to wait until the election was over? If the secretary wanted an excuse he had a very good one in the fact that his minister was away, and he could say that he had no authority from the minister to make this publication. But the

whole thing was arranged, and the minister does not say for one moment that his secretary was not justified in carrying out the course that was laid down for him, possibly before the minister left Ottawa. I believe the minister said he did not do it although I am not perfectly clear whether he said there was no communication between himself and his clerk in regard to the matter before he left. If he said so, I am, of course, bound to accept his assertion, but I do submit that it is extraordinary conduct on the part of- any clerk to take the responsibility of making such a radical departure from constitutional usage in respect to the expenditure of moneys, one of the most important functions of the Government. The fact that he has done this and that he still holds his position, and, apparently, the confidence of the minister, is sufficient to show "that he did what the minister wanted him to do, and that in the course which he took he had the full concurrence of the head of the department.
So far as the question of free freight is concerned, the minister undertakes to justify and defend the course taken by those of his party who were interested. I cannot understand how anyone can put any construction upon the actions of certain individuals in that regard but bribery of the darkest kind. The people of Antigonish are, perhaps, incapable of being bribed, but evidently the Tory party did not understand it in that way. They were told by Mr. Girroir in his manifesto:	Every vote for
Mr. O'Brien helps me in my endeavours on your behalf. He was endeavouring to get free hay and free freight; in the public press he offered to bet two hundred dollars that he would prove something which nobody could understand. In the midst of an election, what does an offer of free hay and free freight mean? Hon. gentlemen of this House who are familiar with the conducting of elections know that the offer of money or of any valuable consideration is a violation of the Election Act and an indictable offence. To offer a man free freight and free hay is not an offer of money, but certainly it is the offer of a valuable consideration. The senator, as representing the Conservative party in the county of Antigonish, offered a valuable consideration in the shape of a promise of free freight, and, at other times, free hay. The Minister of Public Works stood in his place to-night and said that that was absolutely correct; there was nothing wrong about that. He fully approved of the conduct of the senator in doing that; it was just exactly what he had a right to do.

I said nothing of the
kind. The hon. gentleman is absolutely mistaken; he is entirely misquoting me.
Mr. McKEflNTZIE.
Mr. McKEiNZIE: Perhaps my knowledge of the English language is too limited to permit me to understand the remarks of the hon. minister. The Scripture says: ' He that is not with me is against me.' My hon. friend has a wide knowledge of the Scripture, I am sure, and he will realize that he comes within that category as far as the circumstances connected with this matter are concerned. Certainly he was not against Senator Girroir in the language used by that gentleman and the canvass made by him with regard to free freight and free bay. The hon. minister defended the Minister of Railways and the First Minister for any part they may have taken in the matter, saying, as I understood him, that there was nothing in their actions with which anybody could find fault; and he even went so far as to say that the member for Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) was deserving of rebuke for having brought the matter up at all. On the one hand in the midst of an election, the people were being offered free hay and free freight, and on the other hand they were being solicited for their votes; it is quite unnecessary to ask hon. gentleman whether or not that was a proper line of conduct, especially at such a time. Every hon. gentleman knows that any decision obtained from an elector after his having been offered a bribe of this kind would not be the expression of a straightforward and unbiased opinion. His opinions might not have been entirely overcome by the offering of this inducement, but the attempt was bad, whether there was fruit from it or not.
The hon. minister says that the letter which appears in the Casket was mutilated, twisted and practically forged from the time it left the hands of his secretary until it was published in that newspaper in the town of Antigonish. I submit to the minister that the letter was not mutilated by the Casket. The Casket is a paper of the very highest reputation in the province of Nova Scotia for truthfulness, integrity and honesty. It is a religious or church paper, and really takes no part in polities. What purpose would the editor of the Casket have in mutilating this letter? The Casket did not take any part in the election; this letter appeared in its columns simply because it was paid for as an advertisement. I ask any hon. gentleman who has had experience in .the weighing of evidence to consider the probability of this letter having been mutilated. The minister says it was changed in such a way as to make it more favourable to those who would benefit by its publication in the county of Antigonish.

If there had been a
Liberal on that newspaper who wanted to put a Conservative in a hole, he would have been glad to drop a line out of the letter. That would be quite likely to happen.

When it comes to the matter of dealing with Tories getting in or out of holes,-I shall not take issue with my hon. friend. It was in the interests of Senator Girroir and the Tory party that these moneys were being placed in the estimates, should be published and circulated. The heading that was on the list showed that these amounts were noted for the estimates; it did not say they were to be placed in the estimates. That did not mean anything at all; the minister might not put them in the estimates, but when the heading was changed to indicate that the amounts were to be placed in the estimates, it was a different proposition altogether. If anyone were to go to the electors with this letter, and say:	The
minister tells me that he will consider the amounts I submitted to him; he has taken a note of them; that is one thing. But when he goes to the electors and says:	Here is a letter
from the minister in which he says that he puts these amounts in the estimates, that is a different proposition.
Mr. ROGER6:	That is the same question I asked the hon. member for Antigonish but I got no answer.

Now,	whose interest
was it to change that letter? Every body will say it was the interest of those who were using 't as a political engine in the county of Antigonish to change it. That reputable paper the Casket, which was earning money publishing it at so much a word or so much a line, why should they change it? I ask hon. gentlemen on the other side who committed this mutilation, this criminal, rascally mutilation, which the Minister of Public Works says took place between the time the letter left his possession and the time it appeared in that reputable paper the Casket?
I did not say the paper was mutilated; I was taking the word of my hon. friend from Antigonish. I knew nothing about it and asked him who he thought was doing this thing.

Putting the best construction upon his words the minister says that if the letter reads as it appears in the Casket, that is not the way it left his hands. If the change was made in it, it was mutilation, it was rascally, criminal mutilation. And I submit that it was not the Casket or anybody about it that made this mutilation. It is stated here
to-day and cannot be contradicted, that the Casket received that letter from Senator Girroir. Perhaps Senator Girroir was imposed upon. Perhaps he has a secretary, a typewriter in his office who could be blamed for this change. Then we should be thrown back upon some other Gilpin Horner, upon whom the blame could be thrown, and Senator Girroir could get out of his responsibility for this mutilation. But I submit that the fact is that the mutilation took place, and this letter, this kindly note sent by the minister to his friend Senator Girroir, simply reminding him, giving him a note of the things he handed in. Did anybody ever hear of anything more absurd? Senator Girroir was here while the House was sitting, he was back and forth compiling all these statements. He made a note of it. At least he writes:	I forgot
what I have been talking about, and would be obliged if you would send a statement of the things I spoke about. Is that ordinary common sense that would appeal to any person? Senator Girroir was back in Antigonish county. It is not a large county. All these expenditures are within a small circle. The hon. member for Antigonish told us that these expenditures represented over $80 for every vote cast in that election and $16 for every person in the county. That is most extraordinary. I do not say that such may not be necessary. If this is the pace the minister has set for himself, if he is to do the same for the maritime provinces, then even big as his surplus is, I think he will find that he has undertaken more than he can perform. If there is no justification for these expenditures then the blame is thrown upon Senator Girroir, and we have no opportunity of explanation from him. Every part of this case goes to show that this is simply a huge Tory corruption fund and system of trickery with the view of the winning of elections. The country had better look out for the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Railways and possibly the Prime Minister. If these gentlemen are now prepared to go to this length in a by-election which does not affect their stability in this House no matter what way it goes, I ask the country to look out for tornadoes when their seats are in jeopardy, and the result of an election will be to turn them out or keep them in office. That is the time when we can look out for the breach of every rule, for setting aside all the amenities of public life. And if the people of this country are capable of being corrupted, these attempts are to be made to break them away from honest rule and the proper exercise of the franchise which will make this Parliament not the true voice of the people but the voice of the moneybags, and of the cor-

rupting influence of the minister whose particular business it is to win elections regardless of the means by which they are won.
Mr. A. DE WITT FOSTER (Kings, N.S.: It is not often I ask the indulgence of this House, and I can assure hon. members that I do not intend to weary them by any extended remarks. I am very glad, as, the youngest member of Parliament, to say that I listened and do listen always with great pleasure to the remarks of hon. gentlemen opposite. Apart from venturing to ask a question now and then with a view solely to get information and without the idea of being discourteous to any hon. gentleman, I have respected as I have said the time and feelings of the members of this House. I have listened to the hon. member North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) when I think, if I may be permitted to say so, he has done far more justice to the debate than he has done this evening. I may even go further and say that his speech to-night is perhaps the poorest, in my judgment, he has ever attempted in this House. I am sure he will pardon me if I do not follow him in the various ramblings of his speech. But, at the outset he spoke of this case as being one, which had it been brought before any court the judge would have pronounced as proven at once. I submit to any fair-minded member of this House that had the judge been any other than judge D. D. McKenzie, now the member for North Cape Breton, that judge would immedately have dismissed the action.
With costs.

Yes, with costs. On every occasion when a point of law is in question in this House, the hon. member for North Cape Breton seems to be obsessed with a desire to give the House and country in detail his definition of what the law really is. If it was a question of constitutional law or international law upon which we might expect such able men as Sir Allen Aylesworth of the late Parliament or the present leader of this House, to give an opinion that would be a weighty opinion before the Privy Council, we find the hon. member for North Cape Breton plunging head first into the question and giving his version to the House and country as being absolutely final in every detail. It has become somewhat wearisome, but I suppose that is one of the least objectionable features that this House has to put up with from the hon. gentleman until the next general election. The hon. gentleman next came to the point of the denial of the Minister of Public Works and said that the denials of that hon. gentleman were getting rather stale. I suppose
Mr. MoKENZIE.
he would deny that he owed his first seat in this Parliament to the fact that by a technicality in law he stole the election from John McCormick. I suppose he would deny the statement that at his next election some one hundred and ten fishery guardians whom he had succeeded in appointing worked day and night to secure his election.
Mr. MoKENZIE:	I am not aware that
my conduct in any election is before the House.

He denies it in another
fashion. On each and every occasion when a matter has been placed before this House, even on sworn testimony, submitted before a court of law, which proved the case, submitted by the hon. member for Annapolis, we find the same member from North Cape Breton denying the whole thing. I suppose he will deny that again? He does not deny that, because I could refer him to the evidence.
Mr. MoKENZIE: I take it that this is your defence of the minister.

I am coming to the defence of the minister. I want to give the member for Cape Breton a little pen picture of himself. He reads a homily upon the virtue and the great morality he possesses, the wonderful purity characteristics he has in running elections; and yet we find in his own constituency in the last election, according to the evidence submitted to the House, two hundred dollars was paid for rum and liquor in order to ensure him his seat in this House. Yet he seems obsessed with the idea of purity, of absence of corruption and attributes all corruption to hon. gentlemen on this side. I might bring the rascality a little nearer home and I will tell him that the very man responsible for having paid that money was his own law partner. It is nice to have a Gilpin Horner handy so that you can lay the blame on him. He talks about bribery in elections, about it being bribery to publish a card in the riding, wherein certain things are promised. In the card of the hon. member fo.r Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) in the last election, what do you find ? He recited every appropriation that had been granted in his county while he represented it, upwards of $1,000,000, and his friends urged the people both in private and public canvass: Elect him and when the Government is returned he will be taken into the Cabinet, he will be one of the ministers and he can get you all sorts of things. Bribery at election? Promising to constituencies certain things? If the hon. gentleman is so fond of purity he had better purify a lew on his side. Charity begins at home, let him commence there. He talks about expenditure of public money. I have not under my

hand at the moment, but I will get for the House at a later time, the name of a certain gentleman in the riding of North Cape Breton who was under some little difficulty in regard to trading with Montreal and other ports by virtue of the fact that freight rates were not as low to him as to his competitors on either side. So we find the late Government building a wharf eighty or one hundred feet long in order that this man's store might be served and the rate equalized as between him and the other points.
We are entitled to the name of the gentleman so favoured.
I said I would be delighted to give the name later. He does not deny that.

I certainly do; there
was never such a thing in the world and I challenge the member to produce any such evidence. He has not got it.

I told him he would deny
it. The fact remains that the wharf is there.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member
should accept the denial.

Yes, I accept it. Then
there is the question of the manifesto which was issued by Senator Girroir. Where was that copy prepared and by whom? I am not sure that this House is entitled to accept the mere statement that that was prepared by Senator Girroir.
It bears his signature.
It may bear his signature and yet there have been occasions in Nova Scotia where signatures have been attached to documents without necessarily showing that the man had signed them.
The minister will not deny that he signed this.
He spoke of a bet in the paper but he did not tell the House to what bet he referred. I would ask if he referred to the offer of a reward of $200 referred to by the hon. member for Antigonish.
I saw the letter in the Casket offering the reward or making the bet, that was what I had reference to, the senator s letter in the Casket.
As a member of Parliament and an ex-judge, perhaps the hon. member will say whether he considers that an offer of a reward and a bet are one and the same thing.
It calls it a bet, that he will bet is what he says.

I must again leave the
hon. gentleman to his construction of English. The hon. member stated that the Minister of Public Works said that the Casket had mutilated the letter. I submit that the Minister of Public Works did not say anything of the kind, he said absolutely nothing to the effect that the editor of the Casket had mutilated that letter in any respect, and the hon. member for North Cape Breton knew when he uttered those words to the House that the Minister of Public Works had not made such a statement.
I made no such statement. The minister said that the letter was mutilated when it appeared in the Casket, and he did not say who did it. There are only two parties-

I said that the minister had said absolutely nothing of the sort. He did not say that the letter was mutilated when it appeared in the Casket, he said he did not know anything about it; all he knew about it was the letter that left his secretary's office and the letter that was produced here in this House were correct. On that point let me say that the hon. member for Antigonish made a great fuss in this House. In loud words and insinuating language he dwelt upon the point that the letter was multi-lated when it appeared in the Casket. Even the hon. member for Antigonish would not go so far as to charge Senator Girroir with the mutilation of that letter. The hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr.^ McKenzie) when he came to deal with it said there was absolute proof that Senator Girroir delivered the letter to the Antigonish Casket. Where is his proof of that statement? As a matter of fact the hon. member for Antigonish himself saw the letter before it went to the Antigonish Casket and he saw the word ' noted ' at the top. He admitted it here to-day. He knew there was no misrepresentation whatever and the fact that the word 'placed' appeared in the paper instead of the word 'noted' might have been due to a typographical error. The hon. Senator would never think of doing anything like that and there is not a scintilla of evidence to show he did. The hon. member for Antigonish has to correct statements in the press now and again but in de 1-ing with a subject of this sort, it would never occur to him to be fair. His partisanship must express itself, even to the extent of casting insinuation and slurs upon an hon member of the Senate. The hon. member for Antigonish was very careful this afternoon not to say where the mutilation began, but inadvertently I think he made it clear that the mutilation, if such there was, took place in the office of the Casket. I think that is the plain conclusion to be drawn from the hon. gentleman's argument. No doubt he did not wish the country to get that impression, and I think a careful perusal

of his language will show that that is the only fair conclusion from his argument. The hon. member for North Cape Breton says that the senator should have relied upon his memory in regard to the transaction, that as a member of the Senate he went to the minister now and again and discussed the matter with the minister, and that when he went back to his constituency he should have remembered the details and not have asked for a statement in regard to the various works under consideration. Let me go over the facts of the case. Previous to the election we had the hon. member for Antigon-ish going over to the Department of Public Works and endeavouring to find out if any representations had been made in the interests of the county which he represents. How do I know that? That statement was made by the Hon. John Corbett, a member of the Nova Scotia legislature, at a particular place in the county of Antigonish, and afterwards repeated by my hon. friend for Antigonish himself. My hon. friend was not satisfied with that. Before going down to his county he started out to see if he could find whether Senator Girroir had neglected the county which my hon. friend is supposed to represent, and whose interests he is supposed to guard above those of any other community. He went [DOT] down to the county and one of the forms of canvass which he undertook was that the Conservative party would not spend a single dollar in the county of Antigonish, no matter how great the necessity for public works might be, and that they did not care anything about the interests of the county. That was the line of canvass of my hon. friend, and that was the statement made by the Hon. John Corbett at a place called Lenwood in the store of John McCoe, and in the presence of a number of electors Mr. Corbett made the further statement that Mr. Chisholm had made a search of the records in the department. Who ever heard of an hon. member of this House going to one of the departments and searching the records to see whether anything was there which affected his own county or whether or not a member of the Senate had attended to his business? Mr. Corbett stated that the hon. member for Antigonish had made a search of the records at Christmas, before going home, and that not a single dollar was in the estimates, and that statement was corroborated a short time later at a joint meeting at Lakevale, attended by Senator Girroir, the hon. member for Antigonish, and the late lamented Liberal organizer for the county of Digby, Mr. Wall. That was the preconceived line of campaign of my hon. friend, and when Senator Girroir arrived in the county he found the story broadcast over the constituency. What was more natural than
Mr. FOOTiEOR (Kings, N.S.).
that he should proceed to show the people that their member of Parliament had not been giving to his duties the attention required of him, and that he should seek to aid his memory, but not that it needed refreshing, to dispel the disgraceful, lying, deceitful story that had been spread throughout the county by the hon. member. That was the reason why the senator acted as he did and I submit to this House that it was a cogent and sufficient reason, and that there was no corruption or deception attached to the transaction. It was done in the plain ordinary course of protecting himself and the interests of truth and justice, and in order that he should have something tangible to show that he had been making representations in the public interest and on behalf of the people of Antigonish.
At this point let me refer to the fact that in that election it was openly stated that the Conservative Government would not spend a dollar in that or any other county. A plan had been formed to force them to the country this session, and the story was circulated that the Liberal party would soon occupy the treasury benches and be in a position to spend any money that was in the estimates. The plan was hatched as everybody knows by ex-Cabinet ministers, and was diligently circulated throughout the county. Men were betting hundreds of dollars that the Opposition were going to force the Government to the country, and that they were masters of the situation. When the election of Hochelaga was allowed to go by default, so far as the Opposition were concerned, dust was cast in the eyes of the people of this country to make them believe that the Opposition were waiting with an unbiased mind to look into the Government's proposition, and that they would deal with it absolutely on its merits, whereas a year ago the real scheme was hatched to oppose it" in whatever form it might be submitted to the House. The hon. member for Antigonish may take what consolation he can from such statements as were made at that particular time. He says that no main estimates and no supplementary estimates were made up at the time of the election, and therefore that those items could not possibly have been in the estimates. The people of Antigonish are an intelligent class of people, as is evidenced by the fact that they reversed their former decision when the light of truth was presented to them, and elected a member of the Opposition in the province of Nova Scotia, an Opposition wThich gave to a moribund government the greatest overhauling any government ever had since the days of Sir George Boss in the province of Ontario. As the hon. minister has stated, the items were simply in the department for his consideration at a later stage. I wish to refer to that particular point, and to show this House and the country that,

in my judgment there is now a different modus operandi in respect of public works from what existed under the regime of the late Government. As I understand it, today a member of Parliament submits a proposition with regard to a certain work-we will say it comes under the purview of the Public Works Department. There is an engineer in that department, a man who is trained and responsible to the Government which appoints him. That engineer makes a report on his responsibility and then the matter is considered. Under the late Administration, I state from my place in this House, that I believe there were engineers in the province of Nova Scotia who were commanded to do certain things regardless of whether or not these things were in the public interest. Let me cite one illustration. The Canning Supply Company, of Canning, in the county of Kings, N.S., composed of the Liberal henchmen of my predecessor, bought a certain piece of property on the North mountain. They wished to timber that property. In order that they might facilitate the handling of their logs to a mill in a particular creek, they applied to the Dominion Government for $1,000 for a wharf on the side of the creek. There was $1,000 granted by the late Government to be expended in building the bed for a wharf, or what was supposed to be a wharf, on the east side of the creek. There was no public road leading down to it, there were no residents living near it, the onlv approach to it was by a log road across the pasture, and yet that $1,000 was expended for the benefit of the Canning Supply Company to enable it to put its mill down and to take its logs from that particular creek.

How
wide was the creek?

It was not wide enough
for some of these hon. gentlemen to drown themselves if they had fallen in. I could give other illustrations of the same kind, and yet hon. gentlemen talk about corruption and purity as if all the purity existed on their own side of the House and all the corruption on this side. The hon. member for Antigonish went back to the days of 1896 and referred to what the London Times had said. When he was asked by an hon. member on this side of the House to give the date of the London Times he could not give it, and did not give it, and I doubt whether he knows now what it was. Talk about corruption previous to 1896! It would have been far more to the point if he had referred to the one hundred scandals from 1896 down to 1911. But he was strenuously silent upon that point.
As I was saying, the Government refers
the matter to the engineer, the engineer looks into it, the engineer lays his report before the minister, the minister considers it, he takes the matter before council and council decides upon the merits of the case. In certain cases, at least in the one which I have mentioned, that does not appear to have been done by the late Administration. Therefore it is easy to comprehend that the hon. member for Antigonish would not know what was being done in Antigonish because the old regime was over. He no longer was in a position to command a certain official to go to this place and to do this and that regardless of what he considered to be in the public interest. He is a little out of touch with the new order of things under this present honest Administration. I come to one other point and that is the charge which was made against the Minister and to which the minister's answer, has, I think, been most effective. How could he possibly have known the contents of a letter when, at the time it was written, he was 2,000 miles away? That seems to be so absolutely plain that it does not need any further word from me.
Some reference was made to hay in the county of Antigonish. I do not understand, and I do not think the House clearly understood, as to whether or not the hon. member for Antigonish was in favour of the farmers of that county receiving free transportation of hay over the Intercolonial railway. He did not make that point clear. If he had presented a grievance here from the farmers of Antigonish, saying that they were dissatisfied in any respect with the attitude of the Government, or with what the Government did in regard to the matter, his case would have been somewhat stronger, but I venture to say that he cannot find in his own riding any person who is seriously complaining against the action of the Government or the action of any person with regard to the transportation of hay. Several other rambling remarks were made by the hon. gentleman to which I shall not allude. I was surprised, however, when I asked him from what he was reading. I expected him to tell the House' that he was reading from the memoirs or autobiography of the late, lamented Sir Richard Cartwright, than whom no abler man ever sat upon the Opposition side of the House, in my humble judgment. I was surprised to find he was reading from some extended remarks of his own. I am sure that the House would have been interested to a far greater extent if he had given it a list of subscribers to the Fielding fund. He might possibly have conveyed to us far more information upon the Fielding fund than his speech has done.
What about the electric automobile presented the other day?

It was
not presented by contractors, and the subscribers are not ashamed to let their names be known.
If the cap fits you, put it on your head.

If the hon. gentleman had asked me that question loudly enough, so that I could have heard him, and so that I might be asssured he was not ashamed to ask me, I would have told him that out of the spirit of loyalty which we have for the man who leads the affairs of this Dominion, than whom no abler man has ever sat in the Prime Minister's chair, and as a unanimous expression of our feeling of regard and appreciation for the excellent service rendered to this country by the right hon. Prime Minister, the members of this House presented him with that particular manifestation of their appreciation; and I have no hesitation in telling the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Wilson) that we are quite willing that he should publish that fact in his constituency or anywhere in the Dominion of Canada if he wants to. In conclusion, I may say that in my humble judgment the scurrilous, deceptive and scandalous charge brought in the motion of the hon. member for Antigon-ish has been completely met by the minister and therefore any humble words of mine are superfluous. I wish to go on record as being absolutely in favour of and pleased with the administration of the Government of which I happen lto be a humble supporter.

My hon. friend from Kings, N.S. (Mr. Foster), has been entertaining us for the last half hour, but he has not, in my humble opinion, touched at all upon the question which is now before the House. He started out with a tirade against the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) accusing him of a great many crimes and misdemeanours, political and otherwise. He criticised him in regard to his legal knowledge, and told him that he was imposing his opinion on legal questions on the members of this House. I must protest against that statement, because everybody knows that my hon. friend from North Cape Breton has never done anything of the kind. In any opinion he has given with a view to assist us in deciding the great questions that come before us, he has dealt with them honestly and modestlv, and he is not in any way to be accused of imposing his opinion upon the members of this House. I do not think it comes with very good grace from my Mr. FOSTER (Kings, N.S).
hon. friend from Kings to make this accusation and to tell the House that my hon. friend owes his seat to the votes of fishery guardians and people of that class.

It is true; can
he deny it?

Certainly; it has been denied in the House over and over again, and it has been proven to be untrue and 1 am surprised that my hon. friend should mention it again. My hon. friend from Kings is said to owe his own seat to a carload of potatoes. The tradition in Nova Scotia is that he would not be in this House to-night if it were not for a carload oE potatoes brought in from the United States to the county of Kings in order to frighten the farmers of that county against voting for reciprocity.

Brought in by whom?
M. SINCLAIR: I am not concerned as to who imported the potatoes. I do not think there is any question about the fact, because it is well known to be true.

The fact that a carload of potatoes came to my riding is true, but the insinuation that they were brought in by me or the party that supported me is absolutely untrue. The fact is that they were imported by a Liberal dealer.
If my hon. friend will ask for a committee of this House to investigate that question-
Ask yourself.

If we secure a committee I think we will be able to submit proof that the carload of potatoes was brought to the county of Kings for the purpose of assisting his election and that it was so used and that he would not have a seat in this House to-day if it were not for that carload of potatoes.
I ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw that statement.
Order.

I rise to a question of
privilege.
If the hon. gentleman has a point of order to make, I will take my seat.
I want to say-
Will the hon. member say that the canvass was not made in his county, that the county would be flooded with potatoes from the United States if the people voted for reciprocity?

I will say that to my humble knowledge no such statement was ever made, and no such canvass was ever

made that the county would be flooded with potatoes from the United States, because it would be a foolish thing to say.
Potatoes are not a bad thing to flood the county with.
My hon. friend (Mr. Foster), will not say that in the County of King's where the facts are well known.
I will say it anywhere.

The charges of my hon. friend from Antigonish were scarcely touched upon at all in the long rambling speech we have had from the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Foster). He dealt with everything from a sawmill on the North Mountain to the fishery guardians of North Cape Breton, but he did not attempt to justify this Government for their conduct in regard to the question of free hay on the Intercolonial or to justify the position of the Minister of Public Works in making promises to the county of Antigonish for the purpose of influencing the votes of the people. The charge of my hon. friend from Antigonish is a specific charge and it is a serious one, in which two ministers of the Crown are involved. The Minister of Public Works is charged with making corrupt promises to the people of that county with regard to the local election on the 16 th of January last. What reply does the Minister of Public Works make to that charge? He tells us that he is of the opinion that the hon. member for Antigonish will lose votes cn this question when he again appeals to his electors. The Minister of Public Works attempts to give another answer, and that is that he was in Winnipeg at the time the letter was written. Are we to be asked to believe that because, the Minister of Public Works was out of town he was not responsible for what is going on in his office? Is that the position the hon. gentleman takes with regard to the conduct of business in his department?

I hope my hon. friend
did not misunderstand me; I took the full -responsibility for everything.
Why did the hon. gentleman mention the fact that he whs in Winnipeg?

I wanted to correct a
mis-statement on the part of the hon. gentleman from Antigonish.

There was no mis-statement. It the minister is to take full responsibility for the corrupt letter written to the electors of Antigonish, he had no reason to tell the members of this House that he was in Winnipeg at the time his secretary wrote it. The issue in Antigonish was not a
Dominion issue; it was a local and provincial issue. Senator Girroir, who immediately prior to that time was a member of the provincial legislature, was elevated to the Senate, and his seat in the legislature was to be filled at this election. The Conservative party in place of fighting out that election on provincial issues, imported Dominion issues and promised free hay and public works as an inducement to the people to vote for the Conservative candidate. They were not able to attack the Government of Nova Scotia on its record; the record of the Government of Nova Scotia was not capable of being attacked. The Liberal Government of that province has held power for thirty years without a single serious accusation of any kind being brought against it. After such a long period of power, gentlemen on the other side, when that local election took place, had to resort to the means which have been described here to-night, rather than fight the election out on provincial issues as they ought to have done. On the question of free hay the charge against the Government is very plain. Why did they not announce to the' members of this House when asked to do so that they did not intend to give free transportation of hay to the electors of Antigonish. The election campaign in the county of Antigonish began, I think, some time in November, and on the 2Gth of November, 1912, the member for Antigonish asked these questions in the House:
1.	Is it the intention of the Railway Department to allow free transportation of hay over the Intercolonial railway from the province of Quebec to the eastern counties of Nova Scotia or any of them.
2.	What relief, if any, in the matter of freight rates on hay to be carried over the Intercolonial railway for the farmers of the eastern counties of Nova Scotia is proposed.
He received no reply to these pertinent questions. Why were these questions not answered? Why did they stand on the Order Paper day after day and week after week? I cannot say just now how often they were called, but they must have been called many times, and every time they were called the Prime Minister answered, ' stands.' The Minister of Public Works did not attempt to explain this. The reason is obvious. The Government was aware a contest was going on in Antigonish, and that the Conservative party in the county were using the promise to the electors: that if they would vote for the Conservative candidate they would get free transportation of hay on the Intercolonial, if the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways had given the straight and honest answer that they ought to have given, saying that they did not intend to grant this request, the Committee in Antigonish would not have been able to deceive the



electors as they did with regard to this question. It is a circumstantial case and the evidence is so clear that it would be decided against them by any fair-minded, jury. As late as December 15th the Prime Minister said that the matter was under consideration, but we find out when all the papers are brought down that the matter was not under consideration, but was decided prior to that date. It- has been shown that the Minister of Railways prior to December 15th decided that no free transportation of hay would be given; but the Prime Minister, on the 15th of December, knowing that an election was in progress in Antigonish-for I presume he reads the newspapers in Nova Scotia-knowing that advertisements were being placed in the newspapers in the county of Antigonish calling for the farmers to apply for this free transportation of hay, instead of honestly answering the question that the Government did not intend to give this free transportation, said that the matter was under consideration. Then the Christmas holidays came, and the House adjourned. We come back after the holidays, and even then my hon. friend from Antigonish could get no reply to his question. It was not until after the 16th of January, when the election was over, and the Government found that there would be no further object in concealing their decision, that they brought down to the House the statement that they were to have no free transportation of hay. It has been pointed out that the Conservative committee in . Antigonish issued a notice and published it in the newspapers in that town, in which they use the following language:
Arrangements have heen made for free transportation of hay into this county for farmers only. Persons desiring hay can leave their orders with C. Edgar Whidden from whom full information can he obtained.
The following persons have heen appointed a committee to oversee the matter.
A. D. Chisholm,
P. S. Floyd,
Dan. D. McDonald.
My hon. friend from Annapolis has hinted, but has not plainly stated, that the money to pay for the freight came from some other quarter; that it did not come from the Department of Railways and Canals, but from some other mysterious fund of the Tory party in the county of Antigonish. Will my hon. friend be good enough to tell us if that, is the ease ?

I said nothing of the kind. I asked the hon. gentleman if he would state that a promise was made in that campaign that the Government would supply free hay, and I think that by his silence he has admitted that no such promise was ever made.
Mr. SINCLAIR.

Of course my hon.
friend knows very well that it is admitted that the promise was made not by the Government, but by the Conservative party in the county of Antigonish. _ Here js the positive and distinct promise, which I have just read to him:
Arrangements have been made for the free transportation of hay into this county for farmers only.
This was put forward by the Conservative party in the county of Antigonish. How could an arrangement for the free transportation of hay be made except over the Intercolonial railway, which is the only means of transportation that we have in eastern Nova Scotia during the winter months ?
The hon. member will have to keep guessing in regard to that. The question under consideration is whether or not the Government made any of these promises.

Surely my hon. friend does not think I am guessing, in the face of the positive language of the notices placed by the Conservative committee in the newspapers, calling upon the farmers to apply for the hay which was to be transported free into the county of Antigonish ? I quite fail to understand my hon. friend. It was said that arrangements had been made; such arrangements could only have been made with the Minister of Railways. It turns out, however, that arrangements were not made with the Minister of Railways, but my hon. friend the senator went so far as to appoint a committee to investigate the matter and to ascertain whether or not he was telling the truth, and he promised to pay two hundred dolr lars if it could be shown that he was not telling the truth. After hearing the evidence and examining the books of a merchant, tlhat self-constituted appear to have made a written 'statement that the story was true and that the farmers were getting free transportation of hay. In view of the fact that the minister has given us his answer and that they did not get the free transportation of hay, what are we to think of the conduct of the leaders of the Tory party in the county of Antigonish ? What are we to think of the men who stand up in this House and make boisterous speeches in defence of such conduct ?
I pointed out that the charge against this Government is, in the first place, that from December 26th to January 16th, they were silent when they ought to have spoken with regard to this matter of hay. They refused to give any reply to the questions asked, and in the meantime the Tory party in the county of Antigonish were falsely putting this matter forward to deceive the electors. The hon. Minister of Publio

Works has not attempted to make any reply to this charge made against his Government. He does not seem to realize that the people of this country will look upon this as a very serious charge. Regarding the second charge, here is the letter from the minister's secretary, for which he admits he is responsible:
Office of the 'Minister of Public Works of Canada,
December 28, 1912.
My Dear Sir,-
Your letter of the 21th instant addressed to the Minister of Public Works received, and, in accordance with your request, I am inclosing you herewith a list of the items which have been placed in the supplementary estimates for Antigonish county for 1913-14.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) George Buskard, Minister's Secretary.
T. E. L. Girroir, Esq.,
Barrister,
Antigonish, iN.S.
These items aggregate $204,900. My bon. friend the Minister of Public Works said that the letter had not been mutilated. If not, we must take it as it stands, and it says that these items have been placed in the supplementary estimates. There was some discussion as to whether any changes had been made in the letter, but I understood the Minister of Public Works to say a few moments ago that he did not say that any changes had been made. As I say, therefore, we must take the letter as it stands, and as it was placed upon ' Hansard ' by the hon. minister himself. The Minister of Public Works produces this letter to this House and this letter makes the positive statement that these items are in the supplementary estimates for this year. That is a very positive statement, but it turns out to -be untrue-these items were not placed in the estimates at that time. We have it admitted now that the statement is not true, that the supplementary estimates were not prepared at the time that letter was written. The Minister of Public Works has withdrawn his contention that he was in Winnipeg at the time and that that made a difference. I think it was Sam. Weller, in Pickwick Papers, who said that if you were in legal trouble at any time and were afraid of the evidence should resort to an alibi. I thought the minister was going to try to get off on a defence of that kind, but he has accepted the responsibility and the members of the House and the people of the country will hold him responsible for what his secretary did. He told us tonight that his secretary was justified in sending this statement to the electors of Antigonish on the eve of that election. He knew the purpose for which that statement was sent, he knew that it could not be sent for any but a corrupt purpose,
324J
to influence the electors. I do not wish to-be understood as opposing these grants. I have no doubt these public works are necessary, I have no special knowledge on that subject. I am not opposing these appropriations. But I am opposed to a minister of the Crown on the eve of an election sending a letter of this kind into any county, for the purpose of influencing that election. There are a number of questions that may be asked in this connection, some of which were asked by my hon. friend from Antigonish. What about the etiquette of a minister of the Crown in matters of this kind? What about the respect he owes to His Royal Highness in making known estimates before he has been asked to bring them down? What about his oath of office? The hon. member for Antigonish has read the oath of office to the House in which the minister has sworn that he would keep such matters secret and yet this hon. gentleman allows his secretary to disclose them, to violate that oath, and he still retains that secretary in his office and does not even reprimand him but comes to this House and defends what he did, and tells us that his secretary did the proper thing in sending the letter for the purpose for which it was sent. I do not think the Minister of Public Works realizes the position he is in or the seriousness of the crime he has committed. I took occasion to look up May's Parliamentary Practice in regard to this matter, and I found this doctrine laid down that any hon. gentleman can verify for himself. A resolution was passed in the House of Commons of England on the 20th December, 1779-over one hundred years ago-adopting the principle that a minister of the Crown must not use his position of minister in charge of the funds of the people for the purpose of winning elections, he must not seek to corrupt the electors by making promises to them prior to the election. That resolution was as follows:
Resolved that it is highly criminal in any minister or ministers or other servants under the Crown of Great Britain directly or indirectly to use the power of office in election of representations to serve in Parliament.
That is a very positive statement, and it is regarded as the law in England, and I have no doubt it is the law of Canada also. The Minister of Public Works does not seem to realize that he has done something which is described in May's Parliamentary Practise as ' highly criminal ' and was so declared by the Parliament of Great Britain more than a hundred years ago. If the Conservative party are to retain their selfrespect, they must change their tactics, they must either reform their Minister of Public Works or replace him. The people of Canada are taking note of these matters, and I have no doubt that what the Minister

of Public Works has done will reflect upon this Government and will be resented by the people of Canada. The Government may, of course, win a few votes by such tactics in the county of Antigonish temporarily, but for each one they gain by these means they will lose in ten other places. This is not a solitary instance; soon after he took office the Prime Minister sent a telegram to the people of Prince Edward Island which has never been properly explained and on which the election in Prince Edward Island was run. Everybody remembers the telegram to which I refer. The facts were brought out later and the Prime Minister had to admit that he had sent it. Here is the telegram.
A. A. McLean, M.P.,
Charlottetown.
In reply to representations of Nicholson and yourself during the past two months, I beg to inform you that the Government has decided to undertake the establishment of a Government ferry service between the island and the main land. This will involve the changing from narrow to standard gauge on the Island railway. This improved service will do away with the three short hauls, and it is hoped will result in a great advants
The Charlottetown Guardian published this telegram and made the statement that no more important message has come to the people of Prince Edward Island since Confederation. You will notice that that message came on the 26th of December, 1911, and about a week or ten days later the local election was to come off. Does any one 'believe that that message would have been sent to Prince Edward Island on that occasion if there had not been a local election in view? Will the minister of Militia (Mr. Hughes), who I see is in his place, say that in his opinion that message would have been sent if a local election had not been due at that time? He knows that it was sent for the sole purpose of affecting the local election, which was a very unbecoming and improper thing for the Prime Minister to do. How can we criticise his Minister of Public Works, who has the reputation for doing things of that kind when the Prime Minister himself leads the way in violating the principles that he laid down and insisted on for fifteen years when in Opposition? The hon. gentleman promised us pure elections. In every manifesto he issued to the people of this country during the fifteen years he was in opposition, he never failed to introduce the paragraph on pure elections. Yet his first act in regard to elections after assuming office was to send that telegram to the people of Prince Edward Island, and it was on that telegram that the local government of Prince Edward Island was defeated and the Matheson Government came into power. Then we had the outrages Mr. SINCLAIR.
in Macdonald; coming later, we bad the criminal practices in Hochelaga! We had the corrupt promises in the county of Richelieu. What are we to expect? It was no surprise to us that this manceuveringj took place in Antigonish, no surprise that they refused to answer the question as to the free transportation of hay. We knew that the Tories in Antigonish were using it for election purposes. We know that the Government were concealing the fact to enable the Tory party to use it for political purposes. We also know and everybody in Canada knows that the announcement of the expenditure of $204,900 in the county of Antigonish, as far back as last December, -was made solely for the purpose of influencing the election in Antigonish. That was the only purpose for which that information could be given and the Minister of Public Works has not attempted to justify himself in regard to this matter. He will have to give some better explanation than he has done up to date if he asks us to believe that he is innocent in the use that he has made of his position in endeavouring to corrupt the people of Antigonish by election promises. During all the years the Prime Minister was in opposition he promised honest 'elections. How has he performed this promise? Is it honest to do these things? Is it honest as was done in Manitoba to conspire with the electors of a province, to issue blank warrants in order to intimidate the voters of a province or a county? Is it honest for a minister of the Crown, when charged in this House with intimidation to meet the charge with a counter statement that a certain man was a nephew of Captain Sullivan when he was not a nephew of Captain Sullivan? Is it honest to imprison innocent men to prevent them assisting the opposite party at an election?

I do not know that this has anything to do with the motion of the hon. member for Antigonish, but if my hon. friend is going to discuss outside questions, then I claim the right of replying to the hon. gentleman because he is making statements that are absolutely untrue.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: In a debate of this nature when a motion is made for the Speaker to leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Supply, usually great latitude is given to those who speak; it is not the usual practice to confine them very closely to the question before the House.

I was asking my hon. friend a question which he has done me the honour to answer but I appeal to the record of the House to settle the question as to who is correct. Will he say that these transactions in the county of Antigonish were honest and were carrying out the policy laid down by his leader during the

time he was in opposition. Is it honest to endeavour to influence the public in order to secure votes by saying that a certain expenditure has been agreed on when it was not agreed upon? It has been admitted here to-night that while the statement was positively made by the minister in the county of Antigonish that these expenditures of public moneys had been provided for in the estimates they had not been placed in the estimates at that time. The leader of the Government made these promises of purity when he was in opposition. He has not carried them out when in power. I have pointed out to you that disreputable practises have been carried on in Macdonald, and Hochelaga, and Richelieu, and in Prince Edward Island, and in Antigoni'sh.
And in Alberta.

I have pointed out that all these things are a disgrace to the Conservative party, and the Minister of Public Works will have to make some stronger defence than he has made to-night if he expects a jury of his countrymen to acquit him of his conduct in Antigonish.
Proposed amendment (Mr. Chisholm) negatived on division.

House in Committee of Supply. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
Arte, Agriculture and Statistics-Patent Record, $20,000.

Will the minister tell
us something about the work of this branch? I have had some experience of it, and it has been quite satisfactory to me. They have in connection with this branch, what is called the Trade Mark branch?
That is really a separate branch.
I see there is an increase of three thousand dollars. Will the minister explain that?

The increase is due to the extra expense in printing and publishing the Patent Record. The amount voted for the printing of the Patent Record is payable to the Department of Public Printing and Stationery. Twelve hundred copies are published each month, and the expense varies according to the number of patents issued and to the length of the claims. The increase is owing to the increased wages and cost of paper; that is practically what it amounts to.
Who gets that paper?

Every member of Parliament, every senator, and I believe nearly
all the leading newspapers and the principal libraries throughout the country. Of course that does not cover the entire cost. As my hon. friend knows the patent office is a revenue producing branch. It costs about $90,000 to run it, and brings in from $110,000 to $120,000. The revenue for the past year was, I think, about $110,000.
Experimental farms, $250,000.

Have any additional farms
been established during the past two years?

This item is for the
older organized farms, and covers the central farm here, which takes about $110,000 of the amount, and also such branch farms as Nappan, N.S.; Cap Rouge, in Quebec; Brandon, in Manitoba; Indian Head, in Saskatchewan; Rosthern, in Saskatchewan; Lacombe, Alberta; Lethbridge, Alberta; and Agassiz, in British Columbia.
Mr.LEMIEUX: My hon. friend has just mentioned the experimental farm at Cap Rouge in Quebec. I understand it is under the management of Mr. Gustav Langelier, and that it is very well kept, and has rendered very valuable service to the farmers in the district. Some time ago I noticed a question on the Order Paper asking how many lectures the manager of the farm had given during the winter, but I forget what answer the minister gave. I am informed that, although Mr. Langelier may not have given lectures last year, his management of the farm has been quite an education to the people in the district. I would like to know from the minister if he confirms that opinion which is based on information I have received. I have known Mr. Langelier for many years. He is quite a progressive farmer and his farm is visited by many people, including foreigners. Has the minister visited the farm?

I have not had an opportunity to visit the farm. As my hon. friend knows it is difficult to get round all the farms, especially when we have sessions of this length. But I understand that the Cap Rouge farm has done good work, and, so far as I know, the present superintendent has contributed quite a lot to the development of farming.
Will the minister give us some idea of the revenue that is derived from these experimental farms? I presume there is some revenue.

I might be able to give my hon. friend some figures, but I would remind him that the experimental farms are not meant to be revenue producers, and would not be understood as such by any one who has studied experimental work.

But some revenue is derived.
1G25J
Yes, but I cannot give my hon. friend the particulars just now. I could get them for him, however.
I have the farm at Nappan in mind at present.
I can give my hon. friend the general expenditures in connection with the Nappan farm. The general expenditure for 1913-14 is $13,470.

If the hon. minister
will look at page C-22 of the Auditor General's Report he will find something to help him out. There the expenditure for Nappan farm is given as $13,660.65, less proceeds of sales of cattle $4,750.47, leaving $8,910.18. I am glad to have the minister make the statement about the experimental farms not being intended as revenue producers, because he will probably remember the attacks made years ago in the province of Ontario because the Guelph Experimental Farm did not make a profit. The men who pretend to be the friends of the farmers used to make that statement at every election. Everybody knows that this kind of institution, especially when an agricultural college is connected with it, is no more intended to pay a dividend than is, say, Ottawa University. The farm is for experiment, and not for the purpose of selling so many bushels of potatoes at a certain price. It is intended to save the farmers time in making experiments, so that the farmers save the money that the experimental farms cost the country. I am glad to hear the Minister of Agriculture make that statement, and I hope we shall never hear it used again. The experimental farms are not meant for profit any more than are the institutions which educate msn as doctors, lawyers, or ministers. These institutions are the high schools for the farmers and ought to be so treated. Every dollar that the farmers are enabled to add to their income is the return which we get from these institutions and the money expended upon them is an investment that pays better than any other investment the Government make on behalf of the people. In years gone by it has been a fight to have these institutions maintained, not that people did not believe they were right, but because they were told at election times that the money was squandered. I am very glad to hear the Minister of Agriculture give expression to the view which he has enunciated to-night upon this question so that it will not in future be expected that the farmers high schools are to pay a revenue as distinct from all the other institutions which exist for the education of men in other walks of life.
The calf with a cough.

Yes, the calf with a
-cough in Ontario was a strong factor for Mr. KYTE.
some years. I have heard my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) discuss it time and again.
The man from whom it was bought.

Then, the prize bull was another issue, and a good deal was also said about some wagons that were bought. But the education of the people and the education of public men has advanced somewhat since then so that we now vie with each other in seeing how much public money we can devote wisely to the education of the farmers' sons and to impress upon the farmers' sons the fact that they are engaged in a calling that is the equal of any other. I am glad to be able to have this chance to support the wise expenditure of money in this direction. Will my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture tell me about the work that is being done at the Central experimental farm at Ottawa? I think it is well that the people should know about this institution that belongs to the farmers of Canada.

As my hon. friend and most hon. gentlemen know, there is a very large amount of experimental work being carried on here in connection with animal husbandry, field husbandry and horticultural work. A lot of valuable work is being done in connection with cereals, as represented by different strains of grain, crossing and hybridizing, under Mr. Charles Saunders. An immensely valuable work is being done in agricultural chemistry and I think that I may say now that Canada can congratulate itself that it is not second to any part of this continent in this particular line of work. It is being carried on under the able supervision of Mr. Shutt who has been with the experimental farm since 1887. We undertook a lot of new work about a year ago by putting a specialist in charge of the experimental work in connection with forage plants, such as clovers and alfalfas. We are doing a lot of experimental work at the farms, at the different stations, and in the laboratories in connection with botanical study and plant pathology. There is also a lot of work being done along entomological lines in connection with the destruction of the worst pests that afflict the agricultural industry, particularly in fighting such pests as the brown tail moth. All this work is in charge of Dr. Hewitt, the entomologist, a gentleman possessing very excellent qualifications. Then, we have tried to bring about a little further development in connection with the poultry work this year because the poultrymen had come to the conclusion that their particular branch had been neglected. We have secured the services of a gentleman whom I believed from my inquiries amongst the poultrymen themselves to be one of the best poultry experts in the

country, Mr. Elford. We have created a special position for him as head of the department, keeping our old friend, Mr. Gilbert, who has been connected with that branch of the work for more than a quarter of a century, to assist him. We are placing a new building there and bringing the equipment generally up-to-date so as to give this important branch of the live stock industry every encouragement. I have not referred especially to the cattle and field experimental work. We have there about 140 head of cattle, comprising the leading breeds and with both cattle and horses we are doing a lot of experimental work in connection with feeding, fattening and everything that may be of assistance to a man . in raising live stock. I can give my hon. friend the' items of expenditure under each of these heads amounting in all to about $113,000. I can only say to him that I cordially extend to him, as to the other members of this House, an invitation to visit the farm at any'date that they may mention to me and I .shall be very glad to arrange for luncheon. We might perhaps be able to go out to the farm before the session closes.

I would like to have from the minister a very brief statement as to the work done by the Department at the experimental farm at Nappan, Nova Scotia. In that province we have a very excellent agricultural college situated at Truro, a few miles from Nap-pan. I have frequently thought that there is an unnecessary duplication of work and possibly unnecessary expenditure owing to the duplication. If the minister has visited the Nappan farm I would like him to give his view as to whether it would not be possible to have a fusing of the work now carried on by the Dominion and provincial Governments.

I do not like to make
any definite statement offhand in reply to my hon. friend. I am not at all sure that it would be well to fuse the work of the provincial institution and the Dominion experimental farm. Although it is true that the question has been mooted once or twice as to the possibility of moving the farm so that the farm would be in connection with the institution at Truro, I think there are a good many things to be said for and against a proposition of that kind and I would want to think it over very carefully. At the present time I see no reason why we should move the farm which is serving a very useful purpose. I have not yet had an opportunity of visiting Nappan. I had hoped to last summer when I was on my way back from Prince Edward Island, but I was called back
sooner than I expected and could not go. We are extending the work at Nappan.

Could the
minister give an idea of the work done there?

It is work similar to that carried on at the different stations- experiments in feeding, horticulture, 'live stock and the raising of various field crops. The system of these experimental farms is all correlated to the work at the central farms. For instance, Mr. Macoun, the Dominion horticulturist, not only does the work in connection with the central farm but he plans out the work for the branch farms and visits and assists the superintendents of the branch farms in carrying out a certain line of work. By a .systematized line of experiments carried on in different localities we get very much more fuller data than if we were simply to allow the superintendent of a branch farm to carry out his own work in isolation at home without any relation to the work at the central farm.
Is it true, as stated recently in the newspapers, that the experimental farm people have discovered a composition which will exterminate the caterpillar plague?

My hon. friend is a
lawyer and has not made_a close study of entymology, else he would have discounted that statement in the newspapers. Caterpillars can be killed by any stomach poison and the poison mentioned in the article referred to was hellebore which was effectively used when I first started fighting various bugs thirty years ago.
Has the department circulated a pamphlet telling the farmers how to exterminate the caterpillar?
Oh, yes, I shall be glad to send my hon. friend a copy.

My complaint against
this appropriation is that it is not nearly large enough. The province of Ontario is growing rapidly and extending its borders northward for hundreds of miles, bringing in virgin soil, and I submit that in the very near future there should be established an experimental farm in the North which would bring near to the people the teaching as to how to cultivate this new soil under the new conditions. I would point out that in the province of Ontario the only experimental farm under the federal Government is that situated here at Ottawa, between the boundaries of Ontario and Quebec. The next submission I have to make should appeal to the Minister of Agriculture, and it is that there should be established an experimental station in

southwestern Ontario which is possibly the finest fruit-growing country in the world, not even excluding British Columbia. There is, of course, the model farm at Guelph to which something will come under the Agricultural Aid Bill, and the Guelph farm attracts thousands of people every year who usually adopt the principle of going on an excursion in the morning and returning home at night, which, of of course, is altogether insufficient to enable them to learn much of the work that is being done there. For example, people who go from the district of Leamington in Essex to Guelph and return on the same day, cannot devote much time to study of the work on the farm. It does seem to me that the province of Ontario is not properly served in this respect, and I call the attention of the minister to it in the hope that he will -take into consideration the needs of the northern portion of Ontario as well as the southwestern portion of old Ontario, and establish centres for teaching and demonstration in these districts. Ontario is bearing a great deal of the burden of taxation in this Dominion; it is doing so ungrudgingly and without boasting, and it deserves some little attention from this Government,

How does
it do that more than any other province?

I am not making this
statement in a boastful spirit, but it is a statement susceptible of proof.
It is an absurd statement. I do not blame the hon. gentleman for making it because it has been made time and again by men on both sides of politics.

1 thank the hon. gentleman for his bluntness, and I do not know that I need make any answer further than to repeat that the Province of Ontario, by the fact of its greater population and the greater burdens it has been bearing on its own account, is contributing largely to the development of this Dominion, as compared with the province which my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) represents, which is merely a flea-bite by comparison with Ontario, and he knows it. Ontario has been the milch cow for this great Dominion of Canada in supplying improvements and extension of railways in the West, of which we hear so much in this House. The hon. gentleman has prompted me to say that the great province of Ontario has borne burdens, greater than have ever been borne by the provinces by the sea, or by the provinces in the prairie country. If, on some future occasion the hon. member desires to take up this question with me, I will have the Mr. MORPHY.
figures at hand to prove my statement. My plea is to the Minister of Agriculture for further consideration for the province of Ontario in this matter, and I am sorry to find there is a gentleman on the other side, so zealous in his advocacy of his own province, for which I give him credit, that he is jealous of the statements made by me on behalf of the province of Ontario.

The statement that a greater proportion of taxation of this country is borne by Ontario than by any other province, has been frequently made, not only by hon. gentlemen within the Conservative party, but by prominent men within the Liberal party. I regard that statement as too absurd for contradiction, and it never should be made in this Parliament without at least being contradicted. The statement has also been made by men in both political parties that the province of British Columbia pays more than the province of Ontario to the Dominion treasury, and that statement is equally absurd as the other. However, this is not the time to discuss that question.

Were I to adopt the figurative language of the hon. member for Perth when he said that Nova Scotia was only a flea-bite to Ontario, I might remark that it is a flea-bite that feeds a good many Ontario fleas. Ontario is to be congratulated upon the trade which it gets from Nova Scotia; Ontario sends its goods to Nova Scotia, and it takes from Nova Scotia no return except in hard cash. So far as the advantage of trade is concerned, it is altogether in favour of the province of Ontario.
We buy our unshrinkables in Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
And you get good
value.

It has been
announced that the Conservation Commission intended establishing a number of experimental farms in the West, and if that be so I would suggest that the work should in some sense be under the control of the Department of Agriculture, because to be effective the same work carried on by different departments should be co-related. I would direct the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the fact that there are large numbers of Galician settlers in northern Alberta who came in twelve or fifteen years ago and who have become excellent farmers. I would suggest that one of the best things this Government could do would be to establish an experimental farm in that district. I was among these people twelve or fifteen years ago and

since then I had not seen their farms until recently and I must certainly say that they have made great progress in agriculture.
