They are willing and anxious to learn and while I am not making any special claim for northern Alberta as against any other part of Canada, I think we could well afford to have an experimental farm established there, because of the benefits that would accrue not only to Alberta but to the whole Dominion, from the teaching of scientific agriculture to these people.

The Minister of Agriculture knows full well my views on agriculture, so far as the northern part of British Columbia is concerned. On behalf of the province of British Columbia, in the northern portion of which we have not all the transportation facilities that are needed, I desire to say that there is no province in this Dominion which is more deserving of an experimental farm. Every hon. member in this House knows that there are in the northern portion of the province of British Columbia hundreds of thousands of acres of the best agricultural land in Canada, and that many thousands of acres of this land are unknown and unexploited. Every member of this House is desirous that the great immigration coming into Canada day by day shall be well taken care of, and when the Panama canal is opened and the stream of traffic goes through the province of British Columbia, the people of that province will be asked to provide for the great flood of immigration which must come into it by the Pacific coast. Speaking not only for the constituency which I have the honour to represent, but for the entire province of British Columbia, I would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture, who represents in this House a portion of that great province, that there is no part of this Dominion more deserving of substantial aid from the Department of Agriculture than the northern portion of the province of British Columbia.

The experimental
farm at Lethbridge has proved to be of great value to the farmers. It has been said that we cannot grow fruit on th(e prairies, but at the experimental farm at Lethbridge, they are growing nearly all the small fruits with great success. Trees have also been successfully grown, and, speaking generaly, the farm has been of marked value to the people in that part of the country. I would suggest to the minister that in order to encourage mixed farming in southern Alberta, he should attempt to place some live stock on the farm at Lethbridge, especially in view of the fact that on the irrigated land the people are growing several varieties of hay. Experiments
have been made by some of the farmers in feeding hay to the stock, and they have found alfalfa to be especially valuable. If tests were made by the Government at the experimental farm it would be a help to the farmers in that regard. I think it is the custom to place live stock on some of the Dominion experimental farms, and I would suggest to the minister that he should do this at Lethbridge.
I would also like to direct the attention of the minister to the matter oi the pest known as the cut-worm, which has destroyed very many thousands of acres of crops in southern Alberta during the last few years. I can commend the Department of Agriculture, under the present minister, for having sent an expert to that part of the_ country to investigate the matter, but I find that where the investigators found cut-worms, they have recommended a treatment which is rather expensive, and some of the homesteaders who have lost crops during the last two or three years byreason of the operations of this pest are not in a position to go to the expense of using this treatment. Would it not be possible to provide this treatment, which I understand is composed of bran and paris green, to the homesteaders? It is rather expensive in its application, and if the Government could either provide the treatment or advance to the homesteaders the money for its purchase, in order to enable them to rid themselves of this pest, I am sure that their action would be greatly appreciated. I am sure that the hon. minister knows the difficulty experienced by the farmers in this regard, and that many valuable crops have been destroyed in the past few years by reason of this pest.

I should like to draw the attention of the hon. minister to the matter of placing an experimental station somewhere within the confines of the Yukon territory, in the Yukon river valley. We have had civilization in that territory for about twenty-five years and we have been able to raise many of the things which we use on our table and feed to our stock. But wages in that part of the country are very high, and farming, and other branches of science and agriculture has not developed to any very great extent. If we could obtain some assistance from the Government, either in the way of the establishment of a small experimental station or the payment of a subsidy, as it were, to those who farm as a matter of business, conditional upon their making reports to the Department of Agriculture, we would be able to gather some definite information with regard to agricultural conditions in the Yukon territory, and to have before us the actual facts as to what the territotry can produce. At the present time we raise

hay, oaita and some barley. Wheat will ripen there, but it is not grown as a commercial product. There are many kinds of indigenous grasses of a succulent character growing in the territory. During the winter which has just passed, over one hundred head of horses lived out in the south-eastern portion of the Yukon territory, without shelter and with no food other than that which they got by pawing through the suow and eating what they found underneath. I think that is a condition which cannot be duplicated anywhere in Eastern 'Canada. The snow of that district is very light; its depth is not very great, and the horses find no difficulty whatever in finding their way to the bottom, eating the grass, and coming out in the spring in fairly good condition. If these conditions were taken into consideration by the department, I have no doubt that considerable development would take place. The United States Government have been a little in advance of us in that regard. They have had an experimental station in the Tanana valley for some four or five years, and the results which the Department of Agriculture of the United States have secured in exploiting the soils of that valley have been surprising. I can assure the hon. minister that if he feels that he can make a small grant for the purpose of encouraging agriculture in the Yukon territory, he will be casting bread upon the waters that will return to him, I have no doubt, bringing many benefits with it.

(Mr. Chairman, while we are discussing this item about experimental farms, the House will allow me to say a few words in behalf of the county of Rimouski which I have the honour to represent. That county is essentially a farming district, and that part of the province seems to me to have been almost ignored for a certain number of years, as far as the establishment of experimental farms is concerned.
I have looked into the matter last year, and I have written the Conservation Commission-which is entrusted with establishing small experimental farms-asking if something could not be done for the county of Rimouski, and I had an answer from the secretary to the effect that there were five experimental farms in the province of Quebec, already. I think that if additional farms are established in the future, that part of the province which includes a territory of 300 miles and comprises the counties of Rimouski, Matane, Bonaventure and Gaspe should not be overlooked. Rimouski alone has a farming population of 54,000 souls.
I think the Government should do something to help us, by establishing an experimental farm in that district. I pray the Mr. THOMPSON (Yukon!
hon. Minister of Agriculture to take note of my remarks, and if he does not understand them in French, I hope he will read them after they have been translated into English.
On the 13th of February last, I received from Mr. White a letter acknowledging receipt of one of my letters and containing this statement:
Sir. I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of yours of the 11th instant, addressed to Hon. Mr. Sifton, respecting the establishment of an illustration farm in the Gaspe peninsula.
In reply, I have to say that we have only established five illustration farms in the province of Quebec, and, in view of the large expenditure on agriculture proposed to be made by the Federal Department of Agriculture, it is not likely that we will establish any additional illustration farm.
Yours faithfully,
James White,
Secretary.
H. Boulay, Esq., M.P.
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
The meaning of this seems to be that nothing will be done, this year at least. I hope that, next year, those counties will be given some consideration and that something will be done for us. There are five experimental farms in the other parts of the province, it is true, but the district we represent should not be forgotten. The farmers in that part of the country are just as worthy of help as those who live elsewhere in the country, and perhaps more so, because the conditions of the climate are more unfavourable than in other parts where the climate is better adapted to farming.

I may say at once that I
do not rise for the purpose of asking for an experimental farm in my district. I live in a district where every farm is an experimental farm-a model farm. I rose mainly to remind my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy), who boasts of Ontario and of Ontario farmers, that in the provincial contest last year by an Ontario journal, for the best farm combined with the best farmer and the best stock, the first prize was awarded to the province of Quebec, to a farm in the county of Chateauguay. I would also remind him that the dairy commissioner of the Dominion of Canada, in a speech made to the Ontario dairymen in January last made the statement that sixty-five per cent of the production of butter of all Canada was made in the province of Quebec. I merely wish to remind my hon. friend that though he comes from a fine province, a province we are all proud of, that province is not the only pebble on the beach.

I hope the minister will not take exception to my professional call-

ing if I ask a question. Is there any training carried on at the experimental farm subsidized by the Government? Can a man go there and learn what is to be done, and then go back to the farm and put in practice what he has seen?

The educational side
has not been taken up by the federal Government, but by the provinces. We train our own men to some extent, but as a matter of fact we draw from educational institutions experts to carry on experimental work.

I am in favour of experimental farms, but I wish to know 'how the result of this experimental work is distributed among the masses of the people. Must a man apply to the farm to get information, or, is there an established system of diffusing this knowledge?

There is a very strongly established system, as the. hon. gentleman will see by the items when we come to them. We are spending large sums of money on our publications and we have a branch which is engaged in the distribution of these publications to an enormous extent all over the country. These publications are used very widely and very profitably. In addition, we send out men on lecture work and assist in other ways.

Is there an established
practical education? Do the lecturers go around to other farms making practical demonstration of their experiments?

Wherever a province
is carrying on, for instance, institute work to agricultural associations, we are always glad to place our officials at their service, and do as a matter of fact, place practically all our experimental farm officials at their disposal for work in that way. But it is not strictly our work.

How does McDonald College, for instance, work in with the experimental farm? Is there any interchange of their experiments? I understood the minister to show a difference in these farms. But is there any relation between them?
There is no formal relation between an institution like the McDonald College and our own farm, except such there is between all institutions that carry on scientific and experimental work.
There is no affiliation or any definite relation of that kind?
No, there is no affiliation.

The question raised by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) is a very important one, especially
for the province of Quebec. The publication and lecture work have not done what, they should have done. I think .that if purely demonstration farms were established where the farmers could go and learn by seeing, it would do a lot of good in our province and, I am sure, in the other provinces as well. If that could be established by agreement between the federal Government and the provinces I think it would greatly improve the practice of agriculture. So far as I know, in my own county, which is quite an agricultural county, it will be well received. It is a thing I am asked for every time I have the opportunity of seeing them.

In Ontario graduates of Guelph Agricultural College are appointed to districts throughout the province, and so each county or group of counties gets the benefit of the work of the farm through the experience of a graduate.
What does he do?
Does he lecture?
He does more than lecture. He gives demonstrations, as for instance in tile draining.

He gives the benefit of
his information and his studies of practical farming made at the Guelph establishment. A few years ago they sent out practical demonstrators in spraying. In that way information is brought close to the people. But I would suggest the danger of overlapping. You cannot get too much of this information, but there is no use in having it doubled up. One difficulty is that education under the consideration was left to the provinces and the federal authority does not like to encroach on the prerogative of the province, nor does the province wish them to, I suppose. It may be difficult to draw the line between the two. I am inclined to think that the action of the federal Government in voting money and working with the province may help out to some extent. In reference to what my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) has said, I may say that there is an experimental farm or model farm as it may be called at Dryden, under provincial jurisdiction.
There is one at Monteith, but very limited.

I do not know the details but I suppose that farm could be enlarged and its usefullness extended. The hon. gentleman is right in what he has said about that north country. It is estimated that in that country there is from 16,000,000 to 20,000,000 acres of land as good as any in Ontario-what is known as the clay belt, a strip of land through that coun-

try	that will	surprise anybodywho	thinks that that	region is
not capable of raising crops of any kind.
I am inclined to think that a real, live experimental station in that country will do a great deal because while the mining industry there is now of great importance, mining will not last forever; you can only take out one crop whereas in agriculture you can take a crop every year, so long as you pay back a part of what you take from the land. Our attention ought to be devoted to the more permanent development of agriculture in that new country when we know that we have 15,000,000 to 20,000,000 acres of good land there. I wish to ask for some practical information about the destruction of mustard. I know that a great deal is being done at the experimental farms here and at Guelph and we have had a great many experiments and potions and advice as to the destruction of mustard. In going through Ontario I have come to the conclusion that there are many counties where enough land is wasted in the growth of mustard and other weeds to supply the whole people with flour if the weeds were destroyed. Has any method been devised by which these particular weeds, mustard and daisy can be destroyed?

There has been as far as mustard is concerned. We have in the county of Frontenac a district representative of the Ontario college at Guelph appointed by agreement between the county and the Ontario Government in connection with our county high school. The county pay a small part of the salary but the Ontario Government pay the major part. He is available at all times and to every person in the county to demonstrate how best to destroy weeds and to lay plans for draining any man's farm; he makes the plans and estimates the cost, for which no charge is made. Last year in Frontenac he demonstrated on a farm overrun with mustard showing just what it was possible to do. He sprayed the weed with Bordeaux mixture and it appeared that if the weed is sprayed with this mixture at certain times the mustard can be practically eradicated. On the question of experimental farms, the hon. member from Yukon has asked for an experimental station of some kind in that country. British Columbia has asked for one in the northern part of that province and different members have expressed the desire for experimental farms or stations in their constituencies or their parts of the country. We are altogether too slow in this country in establishing experimental farms and stations. Two or three years ago I called attention to what other countries are doing and if you will allow me I shall Mr. GRAHAM
quote a few figures which I gave in this House on April 18 last. The number of experimental farms and stations in different countries is as follows: France, seventy-one; Germany, eighty; Austria, sixty-one; United States, sixty; Russia, one hundred and two; Sweden, twenty-six; Norway, twelve; Italy, two; Belgium, fifteen; Japan, fifteen. We know the very small number we have in this country. If the Canadian farmer is going to maintain his position and successfully compete with those of other countries, every possible advantage and encouragement must be given to him. This is a very large country and while the experimental farms at Guelph and at Ottawa serve a useful purpose, you have only to go seventy-five to a hundred miles from either of these farms to find physical conditions entirely different from those existing at those points. I am prepared to back up any movement which will increase the number of experimental farms. I think we might have experimental stations controlled from the central farms at Ottawa and Guelph. Why should there not be a number of stations throughout the Northwest gathering information there from Lethbridge and the other experimental farms of that country? Why should we not have a number of farm stations in British Columbia dealing with a number of different climatic conditions in various parts of that province, sending expert men to the central school or to the central experimental farm for the province, and giving instructions on the conditions of the soil and on what is best to be done under certain climatic conditions? Think of one experimental farm for the province of British Columbia, a province which is larger than the German Empire, or think of one or even two for the province of Ontario, which is considerably larger than France, which has 71. How can our farmers expect to know all there is .to know about the soil under those conditions. It is utterly impossible. There is no profession which requires a keener intellect or a better brain than that of the professional farmer. There is no profession in which there is more to learn, and I believe that the people in the country districts are eager to get the information. If it were placed before them they would avail themselves of it. We cannot give that information by simply having an experimental farm here and there, scattered over districts of such extent. We should create a number of branch stations under the control of the central authority, and distribute the information through that central point, which is better fitted to gather such information, scientifically and otherwise, than the branch stations.

I would like to add a
word or two in favour of the idea suggested

by the hon. member for Chambly-Var-cheres (Mr. Rainville) as regards demonstration farms. The hon. member for South Renfrew has spoken of the experimental farm at Monteith, which is the only one in northern Ontario. I happen to know something about the circumstances there. That farm is placed on a piece of ground not composed of the ordinary soil of that country. It is placed on high land entirely different from the rest of the 16,000,000 or 20,000,000 acres of farm land in northern Ontario, and that is true of almost every experimental farm in Canada. As has been pointed out by my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), these farms are situated, one in each province. Probably if the conditions were exactly the_ same throughout the province the experimental farm might give good results. But a better plan would be to have demonstration farms in various parts of the provinces. Northern Ontario embraces some 20,000,000 or 30,000,000 acres of the best farm land in Canada, and at present we have no means of instructing the farmers with respect to the conditions in that part of the country. The cheapest and most effective system would be for the Government or for the various provinces, to take hold of certain farms having different conditions, and put practical men upon these farms to demonstrate to the farmers exactly what should be done under different conditions and on a variety of soil.
Mr. OLIVER. My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) mentioned that the Conservation Commission was establishing experimental stations. To what extent is the establishment of experimental agricultural stations carried on by the Conservation Commission?	.

There has been a little confusion in the past as between the work of the department and the work of the Conservation Commission. As a matter of fact, the commission are not establishing what can be called in any sense experimental farms. What the Conservation Commission does-and I may say that I have no control over their operations, apart from being the intermediary between Parliament and the commission- they undertake to collect a lot of valuable data in regard to the farming conditions in various sections of Canada. They have carried on valuable work, for example, in connection with the subject of weeds. They take a number of farms and find out what are the worst weeds on those farms, what progress they make, and how far the weed area extends. In addition, they undertook last year to establish what have been called illustration stations. In various localities they have been collecting data. They select one of the men whose farms have been taken for the work, and, acting under instructions, he carries on certain lines of work similar to that of demonstration farm work. They supply him with the proper seed, or see that he gets it, and he carries out the instructions of the officers so that his work forms an object lesson to the farmers in that district as to whether or not it is profitable to carry on certain lines of approved work. They are hardly experimental farms, they are more in the nature of demonstration farms. They have established I think about twenty-seven of these stations, and I think the idea is to carry on about three more, and to continue the work for two or three years. I may frankly say that when it comes to practical work, work of an executive kind, my own feeling is that it more properly belongs to the department, than to the Conservation Commission. I do not think there is any desire on the part of the Conservation Commission to develop that work on a larger scale. Although it is true, as the hon. member for south Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has said that there is some overlapping, the country is so big and the field so immense, that the overlapping along certain lines is scarcely felt. The hon. members who have mentioned the subject of demonstration farms perhaps do not realize the administrative difficulties connected with carrying on a large number of experimental farms proper. I cordially agree with every word uttered by the hon. members who have spoken as to the desirability of increasing the amount of demonstrative work in this country, but I think that a lot of that demonstrative work could be more properly done by the various provinces. In British Columbia, Ontario, and, I think, Alberta, they are carrying on a number of these demonstrative stations, taking the results of our work that has been approved at the experimental farms, rejecting the many experiments that do not pay, and taking the sound ones, and applying them to demonstrate that they are along scientific lines and might be made commercially profitable. I think that such work belongs more strictly to the provinces, but I would welcome any scheme under which we could work co-operatively. With such a tremendous field we could not help doing good. I may say it was the intention when the subsidy in the agricultural Bill was proposed, that a certain amount of educational work along that line should be undertaken by the provinces.

I think it is desirable
from the point of view of,the Government and from the point of view of Parliament, that there should not be a duplication of work or overlapping by two branches of the service. I think that what my hon friend has suggested that different fields might be occupied, by the Dominion and the provinces working in co-operation, is a very good one. It seems strange that the Conservation Commission should be establishing illustration stations. I think there is

another vote in the estimates of the Agricultural Department for much the same thing. I should think it would be wise to concentrate the effort under one branch of, that service; either let the Conservation Commission take charge of the illustration stations so far as the Dominion Government is concerned or the Department of Agriculture. I never understood that the Conservation Commission was charged with administrative responsibility. I always supposed that it was advisory, educative and for the purpose of collecting information. But, if the Government decides to vest it with administrative authority, it would be well to have it understood. I would understand that the experimental farms established by the Dominion Government were primarily for the purpose of experiment, for what might be called the creative purpose of experimenting with a view to securing actual improvement in stock, fruit and grains, and that their educative work was secondary, which educative work might very well be carried on by subsidiary illustration stations or farms. The primary purpose of the experimental farms, whose support we are voting now, is original action in the improvement of the very foundation of agriculture.
